risk_of_bias.note: The prospective study is at high risk of bias (drug type, psychiatric history and other drugs not adjusted; the amount estimated after the experience; about 70% of the baseline sample not in the analysis; when the day-before survey was completed could not be confirmed, and it could be filled in on paper and entered later), the laboratory analysis has some concerns (each predictor adjusted for dose only; no sizes in the text), and the recalled-state findings are at very high risk (attributions made at the same sitting as the outcome) and are worded only as associations (cards sc_haijen_2018, sc_vizeli_2024, sc_aday_2021, sc_simonsson_2023).

inconsistency.note: More anxiety, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, measured before the drug went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in both the naturalistic and the laboratory source. In the laboratory a better general mood went with stronger effects overall, the anxiety scales included by the text, rather than with a less challenging session; that is a different mood scale and outcome from the naturalistic study's set component, so the claim states it instead of rating it as inconsistency (the certainty would stay very low either way). Absorption's link with mystical and challenging experience alike is reported, not a conflict.

indirectness.note: Worded for the populations studied (self-selected, mostly experienced people planning their own use; screened laboratory volunteers).

imprecision.note: The main prospective coefficient has a standard error of 0.07; for the laboratory analysis only directions are claimed.

publication_bias.note: The review admitted only predictors reported as significant, a file-drawer problem its authors name; the primary studies are cited directly and the review's figures are labelled as summarized.

rate.reasoning: Predictor studies start low, even inside randomized laboratory studies, because the predictors were not randomized; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated, for the direction only: more anxiety beforehand, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in two independent sources measured before the drug, one prospective and naturalistic (Imperial College London, the set component) and one laboratory (Basel, pre-dose anxiety), with different questionnaires, so it is a conceptual replication; recalled attributions in an independent panel (Simonsson et al.) point the same way. That a better mood goes with an easier experience rests on the naturalistic study alone: in the laboratory a better mood went with stronger effects overall. The other predictors rest on single studies or on states recalled afterwards. The review (Aday et al., 2021) is used only for what it adds (the retrospective Russ studies and the tabulation of absorption), since its Table 1 misprints the sign for set. Two further sources change neither the certainty nor the status: an opinion piece from the same group (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018), whose preliminary survey figure appears to come from an earlier cut of the prospective study's sample and gives no methods, is not counted as a further study or used for any figure (opinion pieces are not evidence for empirical claims, METHODS §3.2); and a systematic review of how 25 psychiatric trials reported set and setting (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; a map of reporting, not of effects) shows only that no such trial up to December 2023 compared preparation, sets or settings. A randomized study in 75 healthy volunteers that varied the amount of preparation together with the dose and the support afterwards (Griffiths et al., 2018) is known here only from its description by Strickland et al. (2021) and has not been read.
rate.population: Adults who use classic psychedelics: people who planned a psychedelic experience on their own initiative and signed up online (one prospective study), healthy volunteers given LSD in laboratory studies, and people recalling past experiences in surveys
rate.exposure: State of mind, intentions and traits measured before the drug (set within a day before; intentions and traits a week before; mood before a laboratory dose, personality at screening), and, in retrospective studies, states recalled afterwards
rate.comparator: People with lower or higher scores on each measure within the same study; no study read here compared people helped to prepare with people who were not, and a systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials up to December 2023 found none that compared different preparation, sets or settings
rate.outcome: How challenging, mystical-type or intense the experience was, self-rated (Challenging Experience Questionnaire, Mystical Experience Questionnaire, 5D-ASC, visual analogue scales), and well-being in the following weeks
rate.magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018), standardized coefficients adjusted for one another and for self-estimated amount (about 198 people): set and challenging experience −0.32 (SE 0.07); recreational or social intentions −0.22 (SE 0.08); clear intentions and mystical-type 0.18, visual 0.16, challenging −0.13 (p = 0.088); absorption and challenging 0.22, mystical-type 0.35; R2 0.32 for challenging experience. Vizeli et al. (2024): directions and significance only (sizes are in a figure and a supplement not used): pre-dose well-being with stronger effects on all self-rated scales but three, the anxiety scales included; pre-dose anxiety with more anxiety during the session. Recalled afterwards: surrender r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation 0.64 and confusion 0.58 with dread (n = 143, one of the two retrospective studies, as summarized by Aday et al., 2021); negative mindset blamed for the most challenging experience: beta 0.14, harm thoughts or attempts OR 4.56 (95% CI 2.10 to 9.94), adjusted only for the other attributions (Simonsson et al., 2023).
rate.short: It may. Feeling calm, open and ready beforehand went with easier trips, and feeling anxious went with more anxiety during the trip.
rate.rate: Only links, from one online study and nine lab studies in Basel. The online one shrank from 654 people to about 198 and didn't allow for which drug people took.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_hughes_2010 (ROBINS-I, first pass, critical overall): national before-and-after aggregates set informally beside Spain and Italy, with no modelling or tests; the 1999 strategy that expanded treatment and harm reduction ran alongside the law and cannot be separated from it, nor can the growth of low-threshold opiate substitution, whose roll-out a footnote dates to 1990, possibly a misprint (confounding critical); several series change at the reform (possession arrests leave the criminal count; prices switch to traffickers' reports), recorded deaths follow the number of toxicological autopsies, problem-drug-use estimates follow treatment numbers, and most data come from the agency that ran the policy (measurement serious); indicators, baseline years and comparators were chosen without a protocol, some baselines at peaks (2000 for arrests, 2001 for prices). Card sc_hughes_2012 (editors' checklist, high): no systematic search, authors who are participants in the debate, the comparison with Spain and Italy restated from their own article without its caveat, and figures that cannot be reproduced from its own data. For any effect of the law these biases could change the reading entirely, so two levels.

inconsistency.note: The indicators point in different directions (lifetime use up while past-year use barely changed; toxicology-positive deaths back near the 1999 peak by 2008 while doctor-certified deaths stayed far below 2001), but the differences follow from what each indicator measures and from the rise in autopsies, as the authors argue; they are set out in the claim and are why it is contested, and are not rated down again.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: Portugal's law as implemented within its 1999 strategy, in national data up to 2008 (some series to 2009); the claim does not speak for other countries, other forms of decriminalisation or later years. That some figures are compiled second-hand from national reports is counted under risk of bias.

imprecision.note: Neither paper gives intervals or tests; the problem-drug-use ranges overlap; the doctor-certified death counts are small (about 9 to 76 a year) and, like the death and arrest figures for years without printed values, are editors' readings of figures. Not rated down separately: the claim concerns what the design can attribute, and the evidence is already at the floor.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: both papers are by the same two authors, and the two advocacy reports they discuss were not read.

rate.reasoning: Observational evidence (national before-and-after statistics, and a critique that compiles further national series) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias, it is very low, the floor. The claim concerns whether the law changed outcomes, so its relation is insufficient evidence; the trends are reported in it as descriptions of the national figures, not rated as a separate claim. Counted once: the 2012 critique is by the same authors, restates the 2010 comparison with Spain and Italy and uses the same toxicology-positive death series; its new data are the doctor-certified death series (INE, from 2001) and re-presented school and adult survey figures, which enter as second-hand national statistics, while its judgements of the two advocacy accounts enter as what it argues. Status contested: credible figures point both ways on whether drug problems eased after 2001 (lifetime use rose, past-year cocaine and heroin use rose by tenths of a point and toxicology-positive deaths returned near the 1999 peak by 2008, while past-year use overall barely changed and estimated injecting, HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs, drug-related prisoners and doctor-certified deaths fell), and the critique changes the reading of the death trend and shows that both publicised accounts rested on selected data, so the six-part debate box applies. The erratum to the 2012 paper (Drug Alcohol Rev 2012;31:727, 10.1111/j.1465-3362.2012.00462.x), now read, corrects only the statement that a cited report of the US Office of National Drug Control Policy could not be found on that office's website (p. 111); nothing used here changes. Neither paper has a conflict-of-interest statement; the authors had studied the reform for years, partly in collaboration with the agency that ran it, and wrote one of the accounts in the debate.
rate.population: People in Portugal, in national statistics mostly for 1998–2008: people aged 15 to 64 in the national household surveys of 2001 and 2007; school students (ESPAD, aged 15 to 16, and other school surveys); estimated numbers of people with problem drug use and of people who inject drugs; people who use drugs newly diagnosed with HIV or AIDS; deaths recorded by the National Institute of Forensic Medicine (positive toxicology test) and the National Statistics Institute (certified by doctors, from 2001); people arrested or detected for drug offences; prisoners; with Spain and Italy for some indicators
rate.exposure: Decriminalisation of the acquisition, possession and use of all illegal drugs for personal use (up to ten days' supply), in force from 1 July 2001 under Law 30/2000: an administrative offence handled by regional dissuasion commissions instead of a crime; part of a national drug strategy that expanded prevention, harm reduction, treatment and social reintegration from May 1999
rate.comparator: Portugal before July 2001 (late 1990s to 2001, depending on the indicator; no adult survey before 2001 and no doctor-certified death series before 2001); Spain and Italy, which had made drug use an administrative offence in 1992 and 1990, for some indicators; no modelled counterfactual
rate.outcome: Reported drug use (lifetime, past year, past month) among adults and students; estimated problem and injecting drug use; new HIV and AIDS diagnoses among people who use drugs; drug-related deaths (toxicology-positive and doctor-certified); arrests and police contacts for drug offences; drug-related prisoners; retail prices; and what two publicised accounts claimed about these
rate.magnitude: Hughes & Stevens (2010), Portugal, people aged 15–64: lifetime use of any illegal drug 7.8% (text; 7.6% in Table 1) in 2001 and 12.0% in 2007 (+4.4 points by Table 1); past-year 3.4% and 3.7% (+0.3); past-year cannabis 3.3% and 3.6%, cocaine 0.3% and 0.6%, heroin 0.2% and 0.3%, ecstasy 0.4% and 0.4%; Spain past-year cannabis 9.7% and 10.1%, cocaine 2.6% and 3.1%; Italy 6.2% and 14.6%, 1.1% and 2.2%. Students aged 15–16 (ESPAD), lifetime use of any illegal drug 8%, 12%, 18% and 14% in 1995, 1999, 2003 and 2007 (editors' reading). Problem drug use 7.6 (range 6.8–8.5) and 6.8 (6.2–7.4) per 1,000 aged 15–64 in 2000 and 2005; injecting 3.5 (2.3–4.6) and 2.0 (1.8–2.2); Italy, problem drug use 6.0 and 8.6 per 1,000 in 2001 and 2007. People in treatment 23,654 (1998) and 38,532 (2008). New HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs 907 (2000) and 267 (2008); AIDS 506 and 108. Recorded drug-related deaths 369 (1999); about 155, 152 and 157 in 2002–2004 and about 339 in 2008 (editors' readings of Figure 7); toxicological autopsies 1,166 (2002) and 2,805 (2008); deaths with opiates as the main substance 95% (1999) and 59% (2008). Criminal drug arrests over 14,000 (2000) and 5,000–5,500 a year after the reform; administrative detections about 6,000 a year; editors' readings of Figure 2: consumer offences about 7,600 of about 14,300 arrests in 2000; trafficking-type arrests about 4,500–6,300 a year in 1998–2000 and 5,200–5,600 in 2001–2008; all police contacts about 11,400–14,300 and 10,500–12,000 a year. Drug-related prisoners 44% (1999) and 21% (2008); prison density 119 (2001) and 101.5 (2005) per 100 places. Retail prices in euros per gram: heroin 38.50, 31.33, 49.72 and 50.27 (1998–2001) and 33.25 (2008); cocaine 45.63, 40.37, 60.31, 53.51 and 45.56. Hughes & Stevens (2012): toxicology-positive deaths (INML) 280 (2001), 216 (2006) and 314 (2007); doctor-certified drug deaths (INE) about 76 (2001), 34, 23, 20, 9 (2005), 12, 14 and 20 (2008) (editors' readings of Figure 4); adults' past-month use about 2.5% in 2001 and 2007; past-year use at 15–24 about 8.3% and 7.0%, at 25–34 about 4.9% and 7.0% (editors' readings of Figures 2 and 3); students' lifetime cannabis use (ESPAD) +60% around the reform, about 9.4% (1999) to 15.0% (2003), then about 13.0% (2007) (editors' readings of Figure 1). Neither paper gives intervals or statistical tests for these changes.
rate.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
rate.rate: National figures before and after the law, loosely set beside Spain and Italy; treatment grew at the same time, and some counts changed method. The figures point both ways; both sides are below.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I serious (study card): different samples and partly different people in the two groups, selective return of sheets with an honorarium, missing results, and self-reported, largely recalled readings.

indirectness.note: Shares of positive results stand in for accuracy; take-home strips were used at home on only a little over half of the sheets; one province in 2019, one brand.

imprecision.note: The opioid interval treats 1105 results from 218 people as independent, and with plausible clustering the equivalence would no longer be shown (editors' calculation on the card); the stimulant comparisons were not powered.

rate.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each rate it down, to the floor of very low. Rated as worded: agreement of shares of positive results between people using take-home strips and staff testing on site, not the accuracy of home testing, which no study read measured; whether home testing changes behaviour is a separate question. Status single study: the review's 'five times' figure is the same study (its reference 66, listed again as 92, is Klaire et al., 2022, by the review's Appendix 1), and Murray et al. concerns a colour kit in a laboratory and only qualifies.
rate.population: People using ten harm-reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, April to July 2019, who took home fentanyl test strips and returned results (218 people, 336 sheets, 1680 strip results)
rate.exposure: Fentanyl test strips used and read by the person wherever they chose to test, after brief peer training
rate.comparator: On-site testing of other samples with the same strips by trained staff at the same sites in the same months (852 samples)
rate.outcome: Share of fentanyl-positive strip results, by the drug the sample was expected to be
rate.magnitude: Opioids: take-home 994/1105 (90.0%) against on-site 591/663 (89.1%); difference 0.8 points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9), equivalent within ±5 (p = 0.00275). Crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6% as printed; 27.5% by the counts, editors' calculation) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 (14.8 to 30.1); cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), difference 16.1 (7.1 to 25.1). Settings of take-home use (sheets, more than one possible): home 184 (54.8%), alleys and streets 74 (22.0%), supervised sites 97 (28.9%). Second-hand: difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34% (Kutscher et al., citing Peiper et al., 2019, Tilhou et al., 2022, and Park et al., 2021); its 'five times more frequent at home' matches this study's crystal methamphetamine figures only (27.6% against 5.2%, 5.3-fold; cocaine about 16-fold; opioids equal; editors' calculation); 7 of 70 erroneous or invalid results in a preliminary study (McGowan et al.).
rate.short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often: 28 in 100 meth samples, against 5 in 100 tested by staff.
rate.rate: One study in British Columbia in 2019 compared results people noted themselves with staff results on different samples. Nobody knows how many kits never came back, and many results were recalled later.

risk_of_bias.note: Very serious, as in the efficacy claim.

rate.reasoning: Rated for the question as posed, which goes beyond what the trials measured. Starting high (randomized trials). Risk of bias, two levels, as in the efficacy claim: unblinding (measured in MAPP2, not assessed in MAPP1) with a participant-reported outcome and no reported measure of expectancy, a bias shared by both trials and of unknown size against differences of comparable order. Indirectness, one level: the question concerns MDMA's own contribution, durability beyond 18 weeks, comparison with existing psychotherapy and harms in clinical use, none of which the trials measured directly. The short-term comparison with placebo plus the same therapy is rated separately (low, section 12), as is the rise in common adverse events (moderate, section 12). Contested (METHODS §6.4): credible published critiques and the 2024 regulatory events change the interpretation of the trials.
rate.population: Adults with PTSD considered for MDMA-assisted therapy
rate.exposure: MDMA in three sessions within a manualized therapy
rate.comparator: The same therapy with placebo; trauma-focused psychotherapy; the course of PTSD after treatment ends
rate.outcome: PTSD symptoms beyond the trial period and harms in clinical use attributable to MDMA itself
rate.magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of MDMA separate from expectancy, or beyond 18 weeks: the only later data, an observational visit attended by 137 of 195 randomized, cannot separate a lasting effect from self-selection, unblinding and interim treatments (FDA). The trials' between-group differences at 18 weeks are 11.9 (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) and 8.9 (4.1 to 13.7) CAPS-5 points; 94% and 75% of MAPP2 participants identified their allocation. Advisory committee votes: yes 2, no 9 on effectiveness; yes 1, no 10 on benefit-risk.
rate.short: It's not settled. Two trials found PTSD eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill, but can't show how much was the drug itself, or for how long.
rate.rate: Two trials, where people often knew their pill and rated their own symptoms, and neither compared MDMA with existing therapy or looked beyond 18 weeks. Researchers disagree; both sides are below.

lines.statement: In 36 healthy volunteers in Baltimore who had never used hallucinogens and who all took part at least now and then in religious or spiritual activities (Griffiths et al., 2006; 20 daily and 14 at least monthly; mean age 46; 14 men; 35 college graduates; recruited with community flyers about a study of states of consciousness and a substance used sacramentally in some cultures, and unpaid), psilocybin given by the study under supportive conditions (trial conditions: a capsule of 30 mg/70 kg by mouth in an 8-hour session alone with two monitors in a living-room-like room, lying down with an eye mask and classical music, after four preparation meetings of 8 hours in all whose stated expectation was that sessions could increase personal awareness and insight), compared within the same people with methylphenidate (40 mg/70 kg), a stimulant chosen as an active comparison, the two sessions given 2 months apart in random order to 30 of them (15 per order), is associated with much higher scores on questionnaires of mystical experience about 7 hours after the capsule, and 2 months later with higher self-rated personal meaning, spiritual significance and well-being that the volunteers attributed to the session, a small positive change rated by people who knew them, and no detectable difference on personality or mood questionnaires. 'Mystical' here means questionnaire scores: on the 43-item Pahnke–Richards Mystical Experience Questionnaire, part of a 100-item questionnaire and based on Stace's descriptions of mystical experience, the seven scales (internal and external unity, transcendence of time and space, ineffability, sacredness, intuitive knowledge and deeply felt positive mood) averaged 0.66 to 0.81 of the maximum after psilocybin against 0.21 to 0.38 after methylphenidate, and the 32-item Mysticism Scale total was 252.1 against 174.7 (all P < 0.001; means with standard errors, no intervals). A 'complete' mystical experience was defined in advance as at least 0.6 of the maximum on each of six scales: 19 of the 30 met it in their blinded psilocybin session (10 of 15 in the first session and 9 of 15 in the second; 63 in 100, editors' sum), and the paper's headline figure, 22 of 36 (61%), adds 3 of the 6 decoy volunteers whose third session was open-label psilocybin; 4 of 36 met it after methylphenidate (2 in each of the first two sessions, which included the decoy volunteers' two methylphenidate sessions). The questionnaire on lasting effects, assembled for this study from earlier and new items and introduced after it had begun, was completed by 24 of the 30 (12 per order): 2 months after psilocybin, 16 of 24 (67 in 100) rated it the single most meaningful experience of their lives (3) or among the top five (13) (counts from Figure 3, editors' reading), against 2 of 24 after methylphenidate (top five; none the single most), and some likened its meaning to the birth of a first child or the death of a parent; 33% (8 of 24) rated it the single most spiritually significant experience of their lives and another 38% (9) among the top five, against 8% (2) after methylphenidate; 79% (19) said it had increased their well-being or life satisfaction moderately (50%) or very much (29%), against 17% (4) and 4% (1) after methylphenidate, and no one reported a decrease after either drug (counts out of 24 by editors' arithmetic). Mean ratings were 6.54 against 3.42 for personal meaning (1 to 8), 4.79 against 2.63 for spiritual significance (1 to 6) and +2.04 against +0.79 for change in well-being (−3 to +3) (each P < 0.001). Three adults named by each participant (relatives, friends or colleagues), interviewed by telephone 7 to 8 weeks after each session and told their own earlier ratings, rated a mean positive change of 2.42 after psilocybin against −0.03 after methylphenidate (26 participants analysed; P < 0.01), which the authors call small. The NEO PI-R personality inventory and the PANAS-X positive and negative affect scales showed no difference attributable to psilocybin (no values shown); lifetime mysticism and spiritual transcendence scores were higher after psilocybin, shown only in a figure without numbers. The experience was not uniformly pleasant: monitors rated higher peak anxiety or fearfulness during psilocybin sessions (1.05 against 0.42 on a 0 to 4 scale) as well as more joy (2.03 against 0.63) and peace (1.90 against 0.92); 11 of 36 volunteers rated their fear during the psilocybin session as strong or extreme (none after methylphenidate); 8 of 36 had a period of notable anxiety or dysphoria, 4 of them for the whole session (6 of the 30 in blinded sessions, editors' count), and 6 of these 8 had transient ideas of reference or paranoid thinking; these were managed with reassurance, no volunteer needed drug treatment, 2 compared the experience to being in a war and 3 said they would never want to repeat it, while most of the 8 still rated it as meaningful. The authors, who call this 31% with significant fear and 17% with transient ideas of reference or paranoia, warn that without monitoring such reactions could escalate to panic and dangerous behaviour. Participants and monitors were told that at least one session would bring a moderate or high dose of psilocybin; participants were never asked which drug they thought they had received; the monitors misclassified 23% of sessions (the primary monitor 17%), mostly by calling methylphenidate psilocybin, and the authors judged the blinding adequately maintained because the monitors still believed several drugs and placebo had been given. Three of the four commentaries published with the trial in the same issue, none with data of its own, read the monitors' errors in about a quarter of sessions as a sign of careful blinding (Kleber, 2006) or of results unlikely to reflect expectations (Snyder, 2006), or the stimulant comparison as showing effects beyond expectation (Schuster, 2006), although the participants themselves were never asked. The authors state that how far the results generalize is unknown and that the volunteers' religious or spiritual interest may have made a spiritually significant reading of the experience more likely. In a separate randomized trial by another team, in 93 adults with alcohol dependence who were not selected for religious or spiritual practice (Bogenschutz et al., 2022; funded by the Heffter Research Institute, an NIH translational-science grant and private donors), mean total scores on the same 43-item questionnaire (0 to 1) were 0.59 after a first psilocybin session (25 mg/70 kg) against 0.10 after the antihistamine diphenhydramine as an active placebo, and 0.64 against 0.11 after the second session (both P < .001), with correct guesses of the medication after about 94 in 100 sessions (percentages without counts). Griffiths et al. was funded by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Council on Spiritual Practices, which two of its four authors list as an affiliation, and prints no conflict-of-interest statement. The 2-month ratings come from one study; its 1-year follow-up, under way in 2006, is reported only as bringing no mention of persisting perceptual effects or problematic recreational hallucinogen use in open interviews with 30 of 36. Certainty: low. Status: replicated for the questionnaire scores during the session (two independent trials); the 2-month ratings rest on one study.
lines.population: 36 healthy, hallucinogen-naive adults in Baltimore (mean age 46, range 24 to 64; 14 men; 35 college graduates, 20 with postgraduate degrees) who all reported at least intermittent participation in religious or spiritual activities (20 daily, 14 at least monthly), recruited by community flyers and unpaid, 30 of them in the blinded crossover (Griffiths et al., 2006); and, for the questionnaire scores during the session only, 93 treated adults aged 25 to 65 with DSM-IV alcohol dependence in a randomized trial at two US academic centres, 2014 to 2020 (Bogenschutz et al., 2022)
lines.exposure: Psilocybin given by the study in individual 8-hour sessions under supportive conditions (trial conditions: 30 mg/70 kg by mouth after about 8 hours of preparation meetings, with two monitors, eye mask and music, in Griffiths et al.; 25 mg/70 kg, then 30 or 40 mg/70 kg, by mouth within 12 psychotherapy sessions in Bogenschutz et al.)
lines.comparator: Methylphenidate hydrochloride 40 mg/70 kg by mouth, an active stimulant, in the same people 2 months apart in random order (Griffiths et al.); diphenhydramine 50 mg, then 100 mg, as an active placebo in a parallel group with the same psychotherapy (Bogenschutz et al.)
lines.outcome: Mystical-experience questionnaire scores about 7 hours after the capsule (the 43-item Pahnke–Richards Mystical Experience Questionnaire within the States of Consciousness Questionnaire; the 32-item Mysticism Scale) and a predefined 'complete' mystical experience; 2 months later, self-rated personal meaning, spiritual significance and change in well-being or life satisfaction, ratings by three people who knew each participant, personality (NEO PI-R), affect (PANAS-X) and lifetime mysticism scores; fear, anxiety and ideas of reference during sessions
lines.magnitude: Griffiths et al. (2006), within-person, N=30, means (SEM): Mysticism Scale total 252.1 (8.5) against 174.7 (11.3); States of Consciousness Questionnaire scales 0.66 to 0.81 against 0.21 to 0.38 of the maximum; all P < 0.001, no intervals printed. Complete mystical experience: 19 of 30 in blinded psilocybin sessions (editors' sum of 10 of 15 and 9 of 15; exact 95% interval 44% to 80%, editors' calculation); 22 of 36 including 3 of 6 open-label sessions; 4 of 36 after methylphenidate. At 2 months (N=24): single most or top-five most meaningful 16 of 24 (67%; exact 95% interval 45% to 84%, editors' calculation) against 2 of 24; single most spiritually significant 33%, top five another 38%, against 8% top five; well-being increased moderately or very much 79% against 21% (17% and 4%); mean personal meaning 6.54 (0.22) against 3.42 (0.35), spiritual significance 4.79 (0.26) against 2.63 (0.22), change in well-being +2.04 (0.17) against +0.79 (0.18), each P < 0.001. Observers (N=26): mean positive change 2.42 (0.70) against −0.03 (0.68), P < 0.01. NEO PI-R and PANAS-X: no difference, values not shown. Strong or extreme fear 11 of 36 against none; notable anxiety or dysphoria 8 of 36 (6 of 30 in blinded sessions, editors' count). Bogenschutz et al. (2022), 48 against 45: mean MEQ total 0.59 (SD 0.24) against 0.10 (0.13) after session 1 and 0.64 (0.21) against 0.11 (0.16) after session 2, P < .001; correct guesses after 93.6% and 94.7% of sessions.
lines.reasoning: Randomized evidence (a crossover with drug order assigned at random, and a parallel-group trial) starts high; down one level for risk of bias (self-rated outcomes, expectation, functional unblinding) and one for imprecision (24 people for the 2-month ratings): low. Rated as worded: much higher scores on mystical-experience questionnaires after psilocybin than after an active comparison, and, 2 months later, in volunteers selected for religious or spiritual practice, higher self-rated meaning and attributed change, a small change rated by people who knew them and no detectable change on personality or mood inventories; it does not say that psilocybin changes personality or that most people who take it have a mystical experience. 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1). Status replicated for the acute questionnaire effect only: Griffiths et al. (Johns Hopkins, against methylphenidate) and Bogenschutz et al. (New York University and the University of New Mexico, against diphenhydramine) are independent; the 2-month ratings, the comparison with a stimulant and the counts of 'complete' mystical experiences rest on Griffiths et al. alone, and the plain lines say 'one study' for them. The paper's headline counts pool the 30 blinded volunteers with 6 open-label sessions (22 of 36 complete mystical experiences, 11 of 36 strong fear, 8 of 36 notable anxiety); the claim gives the blinded count (19 of 30) beside them. Not used: the 14-month follow-up of these volunteers (Griffiths et al., 2008), known here only as cited by Johnson et al. (2014). The four commentaries published with the paper in the same issue (Nichols, 2006; Snyder, 2006; Schuster, 2006; Kleber, 2006), the published responses METHODS §2.3 asks for, have now been read in full: all four praise the trial and none reports data of its own, so they enter only as what they argue and change neither the certainty nor the replication status. Snyder, Kleber and Schuster treated expectation as controlled, from the monitors' errors or the stimulant comparison; participants were never asked to guess, and the risk-of-bias downgrade already counts this. Schuster also argued that the expectations set by the preparation and the introspective setting may be an important determinant of the experience, which the claim's wording for supportive conditions already reflects. The only harm figure in the four, Kleber's 8 of 36 volunteers with sessions dominated by anxiety or dysphoria, is the trial's own; Snyder calls adverse events very few, without numbers. Nichols, who synthesized the trial's psilocybin (Griffiths et al., 2006, p. 282), calls the trial placebo-controlled, although its comparison was an active drug; he is not entered. Funding and the funder affiliation of two authors are stated. No doses are given beyond the trial conditions.

lines.q: Can psilocybin bring on a mystical experience, and does it last?
lines.short: It can: most people in one lab study scored as having a full mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.
lines.but: Everyone in that study already took part in religious or spiritual activities, which may have made them see it as more spiritual.
how: At Johns Hopkins, 36 healthy people new to psychedelics took part. 30 got psilocybin once and a stimulant once, 2 months apart, in random order.

Mystical here means high questionnaire scores for things like unity and sacredness: 19 of 30 had a full mystical experience on psilocybin. A trial in people with drinking problems also found high scores.
Two months after psilocybin, most said it had changed them for the better; people close to them saw small changes. Personality and mood tests didn't.
On psilocybin, 11 of 36 felt strong or extreme fear at some point, and 3 said they'd never want to repeat it.
lines.q_on_site_now: Can psilocybin bring on a mystical experience, and does it last?

lines.statement: In a systematic review of 48 studies (1,774 people) of psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT and mescaline, mostly given in laboratories, clinical trials or ceremonies with preparation and aftercare (Evens et al., 2023; AMSTAR 2 critically low), measurements taken between one day and one month after use, compared with each person's own measurements before, most often showed less depression and stress and more wellbeing, mindfulness and social connectedness (changes reported in 70 to 90% of the studies that measured these), and no study found group-level worsening of mental health. Bad after-effects were reported in 14 of the 25 studies that said they looked for them: mostly headaches (52 people, usually lasting a day or two), then sleep problems, tension and exhaustion, with single cases of severe anxiety and of relapse to methamphetamine use. Half the studies had a control group of some kind, but only 14 of the 48 had a placebo group with double-blinding, only statistically significant results were counted, and half the studies did not say whether they looked for side effects, so the size and cause of these changes, and how often they happen with recreational use, are unknown. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Adults, clinical and nonclinical, taking classic psychedelics in laboratory studies, clinical trials or ceremonies, in 48 studies gathered by a systematic review
lines.exposure: A session with psilocybin, ayahuasca or DMT, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT or mescaline
lines.comparator: The same people's measurements before the session (a control group in 24 studies, placebo-controlled and double-blind in 14)
lines.outcome: Psychological measures and adverse effects between one day and one month after use
lines.magnitude: No effect sizes; counts of studies. Changes in 70 to 90% of studies measuring depression, stress and grief; mindfulness; personality and attitudes; wellbeing; social effects. Adverse events: assessed or mentioned in 25 of 48 studies (550 participants); none in 11 (297 participants); reported in 14 (253 participants): 52 headaches, 6 sleep disturbances, 6 tension, 3 exhaustion, 3 visual distortion, single severe cases.
lines.reasoning: Most included studies are pre–post or observational, so the evidence starts low; rated down for risk of bias and indirectness to very low. Worded as an association with before-use measurements. Status replicated: many studies in the same direction for the main domains, though of mixed design.

lines.q: How do people feel in the days and weeks after a psychedelic?
lines.short: Often better than before: less low mood and stress, more wellbeing, in most studies that checked. Some people got headaches, usually for a day or two, or slept badly.
lines.but: Most studies had no blind dummy-pill group, so nobody knows the cause. And most were supported sessions in labs, trials or ceremonies, not recreational use.
how: A review gathered 48 studies of psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, 5-MeO-DMT and mescaline, with 1,774 people in all. People answered the same questionnaires before, and again a day to a month after.
Most studies that checked (70 to 90 in 100) found less depression and stress, and more wellbeing, mindfulness and closeness to others. None found mental health worse on average.
Of 25 studies that said they looked for problems, 14 found some: mostly headaches (52 people, usually lasting a day or two), then poor sleep, tension and exhaustion.
One person had severe anxiety, and one went back to using methamphetamine. Half the studies didn't say whether they looked for problems at all.
lines.q_on_site_now: How do people feel in the days and weeks after a psychedelic?

lines.statement: In communities where people who use heroin or other opioids, and others likely to witness an overdose, were trained to recognize and respond to an opioid overdose and given naloxone to take home (an antidote that rapidly reverses the slowed breathing caused by opioids), the programmes are associated with lower opioid overdose death rates after statistical adjustment in the only study that compared death rates with years and places without them (mostly earlier years in the same communities), and most people given naloxone by a trained lay person survived; how many deaths the kits prevented is not known. In 19 Massachusetts cities and towns (Walley et al., 2013), chosen because each had at least five fatal opioid overdoses a year in 2004–2006, just before the programmes began, state-supported programmes of overdose education and nasal naloxone distribution enrolled 2,912 residents from September 2006 to December 2009 (2,007 who reported current drug use, treatment or recovery, and 905 others, typically social-service staff, family and friends), who reported 327 rescue attempts. Yearly opioid overdose death rates for 2002–2009 (poisoning deaths of unintentional or undetermined intent with an opioid-specific code or the narcotic code T40.6 on the death certificate, all opioids together) were compared between community-years with and without enrolment in a Poisson model with one linear time trend. No community had enrolment before 2006 and all 19 had it in 2008 and 2009, so the community-years without enrolment are all 19 communities in 2002–2005 and those not yet enrolling in 2006 and 2007 (12 and 5, by the editors' count): the comparison is mostly of later with earlier years in the same communities, although the introduction speaks of concurrent controls, and no communities outside the 19 were compared. With 1 to 100, and with more than 100 (more than 1 in 1,000 residents), cumulative enrolments per 100,000 residents, the death-rate ratios were 0.93 and 0.82 before adjustment (the editors' reading of a column headed only rate ratio, printed without intervals) and 0.73 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.91) and 0.54 (0.39 to 0.76) after adjustment for community age, sex, race or ethnicity and poverty, rates of inpatient withdrawal treatment, methadone treatment and state-funded buprenorphine treatment, the share of opioid prescriptions dispensed to people obtaining schedule II opioid prescriptions from four or more prescribers and pharmacies, and year. In the article's second model, by enrolment below or above each year's median, the ratios were 0.85 and 1.00 before and 0.71 (0.57 to 0.90) and 0.78 (0.60 to 1.01) after adjustment, with no gradient, as the authors note; their abstract gives only the first model and calls the programmes an effective intervention, and their interpretation says the effect seemed dose-related. The unadjusted death rates plotted for community-years with enrolment are not consistently lower than those of 2002–2006 (Figure 1, the editors' approximate reading), so the size of the association depends on the adjustment, which includes the time trend. Acute hospital care for non-fatal opioid overdose (emergency-department visits and admissions, analysed together) was not associated with enrolment in either model (adjusted rate ratios 0.90 to 1.00, every interval including 1); the authors suggest that bystanders calling for emergency help, as the training teaches, may balance out fewer overdoses, which was not tested (emergency services were called or present in 106 of 326 reported rescue attempts). The article prints no counts of deaths or hospital visits, no number of community-years in each group and no test for trend, so absolute differences cannot be given; analyses with cut-offs of 75 and 150 enrolments per 100,000, and with opioid overdose deaths divided by cancer deaths, are reported as similar without numbers and without a table (the online supplementary tables, which hold the control models, were not read), and its methods name 75 as the models' cut-off where its results and table use 100. The rescue attempts are trained bystanders' reports, collected when they asked for a naloxone refill: naloxone was reported successful in 150 of the 153 attempts for which this was recorded, the 3 people it did not help received emergency care and survived, and the authors expect that rescues were under-reported. The authors state that their observational study cannot prove that the programmes caused the reduction (Walley et al., 2013). The study was funded by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, with the first author as principal investigator and no role for the funder; the first author is listed as medical director of the Massachusetts opioid overdose prevention pilot, the trainers worked under a standing order from the programme's medical director, and three of the eight authors list the Massachusetts Department of Public Health, which expanded the programme and kept the programme database used for the enrolment counts; the competing-interests statement, which covers the previous three years, does not mention these roles. A systematic review of 22 observational studies published to June 2015 (McDonald & Strang, 2016: 15 in the USA, 2 in Canada, 4 in the UK and 1 in the UK and Germany; none randomized, two with a comparison group; eligibility, data extraction and quality rating by the first author under the supervision of the senior investigator), which includes the Massachusetts study, counted 2,336 naloxone administrations by trained lay people in 17 studies, after which 20 people were confirmed dead (0.9%), and at least 2,249 (96.3%) survived when 4 deaths with unclear naloxone use and 63 unknown outcomes are also counted as failures. These reversals, as the review calls them, count survival after naloxone, not deaths prevented: the review uses them as a stand-in because it cannot tell which overdoses would have been fatal without naloxone, and it cites a ratio of one fatal overdose in every 20 overdoses (editors' calculation: at that ratio, about 117 of 2,336 overdoses would have been expected to end in death; overdoses in which naloxone was used may have been more severe than most, so this only shows that survivals are not deaths prevented). In 21 of the 22 studies the overdose outcomes rested only on what participants reported, and in the 10 studies with unsystematic follow-up only 1,973 of 8,602 recipients (22.9%) are recorded as returning for a refill after using naloxone. The review judged that take-home naloxone met all nine Bradford Hill criteria for causation, but its own results call the dose–response criterion only partly met and give the experimental-evidence criterion only preliminary support, both resting on the Massachusetts study alone, which is also the only included study that used death records; strength of association, biological plausibility and coherence rest on survival counts from 21 studies, consistency on reversals in at least 15 places, specificity on two cases, analogy on other emergency treatments given by lay people, and temporality on 21 studies in which training preceded reversals, among which the review singles out the Massachusetts study and an uncontrolled programme report from Chicago (fatal overdoses fell 20%, 8% and 6% in 2001–2003 after a 135% rise in 1996–2000), from which it says no definite conclusion can be drawn. The review describes the Massachusetts result as a fall compared with rates before implementation and with communities without the programme, and calls its dose relationship significant; in the full article, community-years without the programme exist only up to 2007, a gradient appears in only one of its two models, and no test for trend is printed. The review's abstract gives one death in 123 overdoses (0.8%, 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2) without saying that the figure comes from the nine studies with systematic follow-up, and the printed interval fits a denominator of 2,336, not 123 (editors' calculation: exact interval about 0.02% to 4.4%). The review notes that critics argue the observational data are not strong enough to infer that naloxone provision reduces deaths, and that overdose deaths in Australia fell during a heroin shortage in 2001–2002, before take-home naloxone was introduced there. Both review authors' employer holds intellectual property on a naloxone formulation, the second author (Strang) declares funding and payments from pharmaceutical companies, including work on naloxone products, and a patent registration for another naloxone formulation, and he co-wrote two of the included studies. Which drugs: all 22 studies reported mainly heroin overdoses, methadone was involved in fewer than 5% of reversals in the one study that reported it, and the review states that its results are limited to heroin overdoses and that effectiveness for long-acting opioids such as methadone or many prescription opioids is unclear; the Massachusetts deaths are counted for all opioids together, not by drug; neither source mentions fentanyl. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People who use opioids, mostly heroin, and potential bystanders (family members, peers and others likely to witness an overdose) trained by take-home naloxone programmes in the USA, Canada, the UK and Germany, in studies published to June 2015; for death rates, 19 Massachusetts cities and towns with at least five fatal opioid overdoses a year in 2004–2006, followed from 2002 to 2009, where 2,912 potential bystanders were trained in 2006–2009
lines.exposure: Overdose education with naloxone to take home (in Massachusetts, nasal naloxone): training to recognize and respond to an opioid overdose and a naloxone kit; at community level, measured as cumulative programme enrolments per 100,000 residents (absolute model: none, 1 to 100, more than 100; relative model: none, below and above each year's median)
lines.comparator: Massachusetts: community-years without programme enrolment in the same 19 communities (all 19 in 2002–2005, 12 in 2006 and 5 in 2007; none in 2008–2009), with regression adjustment including one linear time trend, and no communities outside the 19; review: for the survival counts, none (20 of the 22 studies had no comparison group)
lines.outcome: Rates of opioid-related poisoning death of unintentional or undetermined intent (Massachusetts death certificates, completed through a single statewide medical examiner office; all opioids together), and acute hospital care for non-fatal opioid overdose (emergency-department visits and admissions, analysed together); survival or death after naloxone given by a trained lay person, mostly as reported by participants (review)
lines.magnitude: Walley et al. (2013), full article: opioid overdose death-rate ratios against community-years without enrolment (all 19 communities in 2002–2005, and 12 in 2006 and 5 in 2007 by the editors' count; none in 2008–2009), from Poisson models with one linear time trend (crude is the editors' reading of a column headed only rate ratio, printed without intervals): absolute model, 1–100 enrolments per 100,000, crude 0.93, adjusted 0.73 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.91), P<0.01; more than 100 per 100,000, crude 0.82, adjusted 0.54 (0.39 to 0.76), P<0.01; relative model, below each year's median, crude 0.85, adjusted 0.71 (0.57 to 0.90), P<0.01; above it, crude 1.00, adjusted 0.78 (0.60 to 1.01), P=0.06. Acute hospital care for non-fatal opioid overdose, adjusted: 0.93 (0.80 to 1.08) and 0.92 (0.75 to 1.13) in the absolute model, 0.90 (0.76 to 1.07) and 1.00 (0.86 to 1.16) in the relative model. 2,912 enrolled and 327 rescue attempts reported, 2006–2009; naloxone reported successful in 150 of the 153 attempts with this recorded. No death or event counts, community-years per group or test for trend printed, so no absolute difference. McDonald & Strang (2016): 2,336 lay naloxone administrations in 17 studies; 20 confirmed deaths afterwards (0.9%, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2), 24 including 4 with unclear naloxone use (1.0%, 0.6 to 1.4); at least 2,249 survivals (96.3%, 95.5 to 97.1); one death in 123 administrations in the nine studies with systematic follow-up (0.8%, printed 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2; editors' calculation: exact interval 0.02% to 4.4%); ratio of one fatal overdose per 20 overdoses cited (editors' calculation: about 117 of 2,336 expected deaths at that ratio). Deaths prevented: not known.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (an ecological time series in which most of the comparison is of later with earlier years in the same communities, through one linear time trend, and whose association is much weaker before adjustment; and survival counts without comparison) and one for indirectness (survival after naloxone stands in for deaths prevented; heroin, not fentanyl): very low. Rated as worded: an association between programme roll-out and lower opioid overdose death rates in one US state, and survival after naloxone given by trained lay people; the claim does not say that the kits prevented any number of deaths, which no study read could measure. Revisited after the full article of Walley et al. (2013) was read (the earlier versions rested on the BMJ's one-page print summary): the rating stays very low. The full article adds that all 19 communities had the programme in 2008–2009, that its second exposure model shows no gradient, that the unadjusted death rates it plots are not consistently lower with enrolment, that acute hospital care showed no association, and that no death counts are printed; a strict reading would rate risk of bias down two levels for the death-rate evidence, which would leave the certainty at very low, the lowest level. Overlap: the review includes the Massachusetts study, on which its dose–response and experimental-evidence judgments and its community-level mortality conclusion rest entirely, so the two sources are not independent for deaths. The review's other studies support that trained lay people used naloxone and that most people given it survived, not how many deaths were prevented; its judgment that all nine Bradford Hill criteria are met is reported as its judgment, with its own qualifications (dose–response only partly met, experimental evidence preliminary). Its abstract interval for one death in 123 is not used as printed (editors' recalculation in the statement). 'Is associated with', not 'reduces', at very low certainty (METHODS §6.1). Status single study: only one study compared death rates with a comparison. A review of fatal heroin overdoses in Victoria, Australia, listed in the project's harm-reduction list as a counter-case to take-home naloxone (Stam et al., 2018), is not on file; read it before this claim leaves draft.

lines.q: Does giving out naloxone kits prevent opioid overdose deaths?
lines.short: Naloxone kits are linked to fewer deaths from heroin and other opioids, but it's not proven. At least 96 in 100 people given naloxone by someone trained survived.
lines.but: Surviving doesn't prove naloxone saved a life, since most overdoses aren't fatal, and only one study compared death rates.
how: In 19 Massachusetts towns, 2006 to 2009, 2,912 people who might see an opioid overdose got training and nasal naloxone. They reported 327 rescue attempts.
Where more than 1 in 1,000 people were trained, opioid death rates were about a fifth lower, and nearly half lower after allowing for other differences.
Every town had the programme by 2008, so the study mostly compared later years with earlier ones. It never printed how many people died.
Trained people gave naloxone 2,336 times, mostly for heroin overdoses; 20 are known to have died. Since most overdoses aren't fatal, lives saved are unknown.
lines.q_on_site_now: Does giving out naloxone kits prevent opioid overdose deaths?

lines.statement: In adults who planned, on their own initiative, to take a classic psychedelic, a better state of mind measured before the drug is associated with a less challenging experience, and in laboratory LSD sessions mood and personality measured before the dose were associated with how the session went; many of the larger associations reported come from people recalling afterwards how they had felt. In the only prospective study outside a laboratory among these sources (Haijen et al., 2018; self-selected adults who answered online surveys; of the 379 who reported back, 48% took LSD or 1P-LSD, 29% psilocybin and 11% ayahuasca), feeling comfortable, open, well prepared, not anxious and in a good mood, rated by the participants within the day before ('set'), went with lower Challenging Experience Questionnaire scores they gave about a day after (standardized beta −0.32, SE 0.07; moderate in the editors' terms), as did recreational or social intentions rated a week before (−0.22; small). Strong expectations and a clear intention went with higher mystical-type (0.18) and visual (0.16) scores but not clearly with challenge, and set was unrelated to mystical-type scores. The trait absorption went with more intense experiences of every kind, challenging (0.22) as well as mystical-type (0.35), while trait anxiety, openness, emotional stability, suggestibility and the number of earlier psychedelic experiences showed no statistically significant association with any of them in this model of about 198 people. The sample shrank from 654 a week before to about 198 in this analysis (editors' inference), and the predictors were adjusted for one another and for an amount the participants estimated after the experience, not for the drug taken or psychiatric history. Average well-being rose from 49.0 before to 52.6 two weeks after, with no comparison group and fewer than half the sample remaining, and mystical-type scores no longer predicted it once traits, intentions, set and setting were in the model. In healthy volunteers given LSD, mostly lying in bed in a quiet hospital room and mostly with a placebo session for comparison (nine Basel laboratory studies, 213 people; Vizeli et al., 2024), higher well-being rated on a mood questionnaire before the dose went with stronger effects on every self-rated scale except a rating of a bad drug effect and two others, the anxiety scales included, so in these sessions a better mood went with a stronger experience rather than a less challenging one; anxiety rated before the dose went with more anxiety during the session, and openness with more mystical-type ratings, all at a given dose; the text gives no sizes. In two retrospective studies of people who had used psilocybin, as summarized by a systematic review the editors rate critically low (Aday et al., 2021), states recalled after the experience were associated with it; in the one for which the review gives figures (143 people), surrender correlated with mystical-type experience (r = 0.72) and preoccupation and confusion with dread (0.64 and 0.58). In a US online panel, people who blamed a negative mindset for their most challenging experience rated it as more challenging (beta 0.14) and more often reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others afterwards (odds ratio 4.56, 95% CI 2.10 to 9.94, adjusted only for the other circumstances respondents could tick; 41 of the 613 reported any; Simonsson et al., 2023). Such recalled states are associations reported by the same people at the same sitting, not predictors. An opinion piece by the same research group as the prospective study (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018) previewed, in one figure and without methods, preliminary models from what appears to be an earlier cut of the same online survey (266 people who completed four surveys): readiness, a clear intention with strong expectations, and trust in the people who would be present, all rated before the experience, went with less challenging experiences; because it gives no named outcome measures or full measurement details, sample description or model details and its sample appears to overlap the prospective study's, it is not counted as a further study and its figures are not used. Preparation is routine in clinical trials, but none of those reviewed compared different kinds of it: a systematic review of 25 trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders, published up to December 2023 (Estric et al., 2025; it mapped what the trials reported, without appraising them or combining their outcomes), found that 21 described giving information about the effects, 19 meetings beforehand to build trust (mostly one to four, of about 2 hours each) and 18 advice on the attitude to take, mostly openness and letting go, and that no included trial compared different preparation, sets or settings; the review's remark that one trial's two-interview preparation made the experience and its benefits greater rests on a trial that did not vary preparation. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Adults who use classic psychedelics: people who planned a psychedelic experience on their own initiative and signed up online (one prospective study), healthy volunteers given LSD in laboratory studies, and people recalling past experiences in surveys
lines.exposure: State of mind, intentions and traits measured before the drug (set within a day before; intentions and traits a week before; mood before a laboratory dose, personality at screening), and, in retrospective studies, states recalled afterwards
lines.comparator: People with lower or higher scores on each measure within the same study; no study read here compared people helped to prepare with people who were not, and a systematic review of 25 psychiatric trials up to December 2023 found none that compared different preparation, sets or settings
lines.outcome: How challenging, mystical-type or intense the experience was, self-rated (Challenging Experience Questionnaire, Mystical Experience Questionnaire, 5D-ASC, visual analogue scales), and well-being in the following weeks
lines.magnitude: Haijen et al. (2018), standardized coefficients adjusted for one another and for self-estimated amount (about 198 people): set and challenging experience −0.32 (SE 0.07); recreational or social intentions −0.22 (SE 0.08); clear intentions and mystical-type 0.18, visual 0.16, challenging −0.13 (p = 0.088); absorption and challenging 0.22, mystical-type 0.35; R2 0.32 for challenging experience. Vizeli et al. (2024): directions and significance only (sizes are in a figure and a supplement not used): pre-dose well-being with stronger effects on all self-rated scales but three, the anxiety scales included; pre-dose anxiety with more anxiety during the session. Recalled afterwards: surrender r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation 0.64 and confusion 0.58 with dread (n = 143, one of the two retrospective studies, as summarized by Aday et al., 2021); negative mindset blamed for the most challenging experience: beta 0.14, harm thoughts or attempts OR 4.56 (95% CI 2.10 to 9.94), adjusted only for the other attributions (Simonsson et al., 2023).
lines.reasoning: Predictor studies start low, even inside randomized laboratory studies, because the predictors were not randomized; down one for risk of bias, giving very low. Status replicated, for the direction only: more anxiety beforehand, alone or within a worse overall state of mind, went with a more anxious or more challenging experience in two independent sources measured before the drug, one prospective and naturalistic (Imperial College London, the set component) and one laboratory (Basel, pre-dose anxiety), with different questionnaires, so it is a conceptual replication; recalled attributions in an independent panel (Simonsson et al.) point the same way. That a better mood goes with an easier experience rests on the naturalistic study alone: in the laboratory a better mood went with stronger effects overall. The other predictors rest on single studies or on states recalled afterwards. The review (Aday et al., 2021) is used only for what it adds (the retrospective Russ studies and the tabulation of absorption), since its Table 1 misprints the sign for set. Two further sources change neither the certainty nor the status: an opinion piece from the same group (Carhart-Harris et al., 2018), whose preliminary survey figure appears to come from an earlier cut of the prospective study's sample and gives no methods, is not counted as a further study or used for any figure (opinion pieces are not evidence for empirical claims, METHODS §3.2); and a systematic review of how 25 psychiatric trials reported set and setting (Estric et al., 2025; AMSTAR 2 critically low; a map of reporting, not of effects) shows only that no such trial up to December 2023 compared preparation, sets or settings. A randomized study in 75 healthy volunteers that varied the amount of preparation together with the dose and the support afterwards (Griffiths et al., 2018) is known here only from its description by Strickland et al. (2021) and has not been read.

lines.q: Does how I feel beforehand change how a psychedelic trip goes?
lines.short: It may. Feeling calm, open and ready beforehand went with easier trips, and feeling anxious went with more anxiety during the trip.
lines.but: These are links: no study we read changed how people felt beforehand to test it.
how: About 650 people planning their own trip answered surveys; about 200 answered enough to be counted. Those who felt calm, open and ready the day before said the trip was less hard.
In lab studies of LSD, feeling anxious before the dose went with more anxiety. Feeling well went with stronger effects overall, not easier ones.
Bigger links come from people looking back on how they'd felt, asked at the same time as how the trip went, so they don't show what came first.
Clinical trials prepare people with meetings and advice. But a review of 25 trials found none that compared different ways of preparing.
lines.q_on_site_now: Does how I feel beforehand change how a psychedelic trip goes?

lines.statement: In people who had used magic mushrooms (mushrooms containing psilocybin) in the past 12 months and took part in the Global Drug Survey 2017, an anonymous online survey of drug use open from November 2016 to January 2017 in 10 languages, which people chose to join through social networks, media partners and harm-reduction organisations and were not paid for (12,534 respondents reported past-year use: 62.9% were under 25, 78.7% men, and most lived in Germany, the United States, Canada, Denmark or the United Kingdom), 19 of the 9,233 who answered the question (0.2%; about 2 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency medical treatment after using magic mushrooms in that year (Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al., 2022). The denominator is the people who answered that question (74% of those reporting past-year use, editors' calculation), not everyone who reported past-year use, although the abstract describes the 9,233 as the past-year group; among the 1,895 who completed the whole survey, 1,857 answered and 6 (0.3%) said yes, which the authors read as showing that most missing answers came from people who left the survey early. Emergency treatment was not defined, answers were not checked against any record, and the number of incidents per person was not asked; dividing the 19 people by an estimated 34,347 days of use (a mean of 3.72 days a year), the authors put the figure at about 1 in 1,800 past-year intakes (0.06%). In the companion analysis of the same survey, 102 of 10,293 people who had used LSD in the past year and answered (1.0%; about 10 in 1,000) said they had sought emergency treatment after LSD, which the authors describe as about five times the mushroom share (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022); per day of use, the LSD figure is about 3.4 times the mushroom figure (editors' calculation). Of the 19, 8 (42%) said they had been admitted to hospital, which the survey did not define (as the LSD paper states). They ticked a median of 5 symptoms from a list of 21: anxiety or panic 68%, paranoia 68%, seeing or hearing things 42%, passing out 37%, difficulty breathing 32% and seizures 26% (13, 13, 8, 7, 6 and 5 of the 19 by the editors' arithmetic, matching the bars of a figure that prints no values; in the same figure about 1 of the 19 ticked thoughts or acts of self-harm); the authors note that passing out may in some cases have been brief memory loss or falling asleep, and that they cannot confirm that the seizures were epileptic rather than triggered by psychological factors. Of the 18 who said how long it took to feel back to normal, 17 did so within 24 hours (12 within 6 hours) and 1 within 5 to 7 days; the authors add that 'back to normal' may for some have meant only that the acute effects had resolved. In the session that led to emergency treatment, 8 of the 19 had taken nothing else and 11 (editors' subtraction) had also taken another substance, most often cannabis (7) or alcohol (6); how often people combined substances in sessions that did not end in emergency treatment was not asked. Choosing up to three of six reasons, with no 'other' option, they named their mood or mindset (9), mixing substances (7), the place or setting (7) or taking too much (5), or did not know (4); 1 thought the drug had not been magic mushrooms. The people who sought treatment were younger (median age 19 against 23; p = 0.002); with 19 events, no difference was detected by sex, lifetime mental health diagnosis, first use in the past year, usual quantity or frequency of use. Afterwards, 58% said they had cut down their use and 37% that it had not changed. The authors write that the results 'confirm psilocybin mushrooms are a relatively safe drug' and that harm-reduction information probably does much to prevent adverse effects; the survey cannot count deaths, lasting harm or people who could not or did not answer, and harm-reduction information was not studied. The survey's founder and owner is an author; King's College London receives funding from COMPASS Pathways for psilocybin trials led by two of the authors, one of whom (Rucker) has been paid as a consultant by Clerkenwell Health and Beckley PsyTech, and the other (Young) has had honoraria and consulting fees from several drug companies and co-edits the publishing journal; the funding statement names UK National Institute for Health Research support for those two authors and no funder for the survey. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Respondents to the Global Drug Survey 2017 (anonymous, online, self-nominated; November 2016 to January 2017; 10 languages) who reported magic mushroom use in the past 12 months (12,534; 62.9% under 25, 78.7% men, most living in Germany, the United States, Canada, Denmark or the United Kingdom), of whom 9,233 answered the emergency-treatment question
lines.exposure: Use of magic mushrooms (psilocybin-containing mushrooms) in the past 12 months, self-reported; species, potency and content unknown; other substances in the incident session as reported
lines.comparator: None outside the sample: within it, respondents who answered and did not report seeking emergency treatment (for age, sex, mental health diagnosis, first use, usual quantity and frequency of use); in the companion analysis of the same survey, respondents who had used LSD
lines.outcome: Self-reported seeking of emergency medical treatment (not defined) after magic mushroom use in the past 12 months; for those who said yes, symptoms ticked from a list of 21, self-reported hospital admission (not defined), time to feel back to normal, other substances in that session, perceived reasons and change in use
lines.magnitude: Kopra, Ferris, Winstock, et al. (2022): 19 of 9,233 who answered (0.2%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 0.13% to 0.32%); completers 6 of 1,857 (0.3%); per day of use 0.00055 (0.06%, about 1 in 1,800; 19 divided by an estimated 34,347 days). Of the 19: hospital admission 8 (42%; printed 95% CI 20–64%; editors' Wilson 23% to 64%); anxiety or panic 68%, paranoia 68%, seeing or hearing things 42%, passing out 37%, difficulty breathing 32%, seizures 26%; back to normal within 24 hours 17 of 18, within 5 to 7 days 18 of 18; nothing else taken 8, cannabis 7, alcohol 6; reasons mood or mindset 9, mixing 7, setting 7, too much 5, don't know 4, not magic mushrooms 1; median age 19 against 23 (p = 0.002). Companion LSD analysis (Kopra, Ferris, Rucker, et al., 2022): 102 of 10,293 (1.0%); editors' calculation: about 4.8 times the mushroom share per person and about 3.4 times per day of use.
lines.reasoning: A descriptive claim, rated as a description of the population sampled (METHODS §6.3): starts low; down one for measurement (risk of bias) and one for coverage (indirectness), giving very low, the floor; never upgraded. 'Describes' because it reports how many respondents said they had sought emergency treatment, not a risk for people who use magic mushrooms and not a cause of the symptoms. The question is worded with 'seek', not 'need', because the survey asked whether people had sought emergency treatment, not whether they needed it. Status single study: one survey wave; the LSD figure comes from a companion analysis of the same survey by the same team and is a comparison within that survey, not a replication. The per-day figure is the authors' calculation and counts each person once. The authors' conclusions that the results confirm relative safety and that harm-reduction information plays a key role are not adopted: the survey could not count deaths or people who did not answer, and harm-reduction information was not studied. Numbers of mushrooms are left out, and 'taking too much' appears only as a reason respondents chose.

lines.q: How often do people seek emergency treatment after magic mushrooms?
lines.short: About 2 in 1,000 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After LSD: 10 in 1,000.
lines.but: Volunteers answered an online survey about themselves; nobody checked their answers, and people who could not answer were not counted.
how: In the 2017 Global Drug Survey, 9,233 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year answered this question; 19 said yes.
Of the 19, 13 reported anxiety or panic and 13 paranoia; 8 said they were admitted to hospital.
17 of the 18 who answered felt back to normal within a day, and all within a week.
Those who sought treatment were younger: typically 19, against 23 for the others who answered.
lines.q_on_site_now: How often do people seek emergency treatment after magic mushrooms?

lines.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether decriminalising the possession of all illegal drugs for personal use in Portugal, from cannabis to heroin and cocaine, changed drug use, drug deaths, HIV or the load on police and prisons. The law, in force from 1 July 2001, made acquiring, possessing or using up to ten days' supply an administrative offence dealt with by regional dissuasion commissions (panels of three that can refer people to treatment or impose sanctions such as fines) instead of a crime punishable by up to a year in prison; possession for supply stayed a crime. It came two years after a national drug strategy began expanding prevention, harm reduction, treatment and social reintegration (May 1999), and no study read compares Portugal with a modelled counterfactual. In national statistics compiled by two researchers who had studied the reform for years, set beside Spain and Italy where data allowed, without statistical tests (Hughes & Stevens, 2010), the share of people aged 15 to 64 who had ever used an illegal drug rose from 7.8% in 2001 (7.6% in the paper's table) to 12.0% in 2007, while use in the past year went from 3.4% to 3.7% (cannabis 3.3% to 3.6%, cocaine 0.3% to 0.6%, heroin 0.2% to 0.3%); there was no national survey before 2001, the paper does not say when in 2001 the first one was done, and past-year cannabis and cocaine use also rose in Spain and Italy. Among school students aged 15 to 16, lifetime use of any illegal drug was about 12% in 1999, 18% in 2003 and 14% in 2007 (editors' reading of a figure). Estimated problem drug use went from 7.6 to 6.8 per 1,000 people aged 15 to 64 between 2000 and 2005, within overlapping ranges that the authors say make the fall not statistically significant, and estimated injecting drug use from 3.5 to 2.0 per 1,000; both estimates are derived from numbers in treatment, which rose from 23,654 people in 1998 to 38,532 in 2008. New HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs fell from 907 in 2000 to 267 in 2008 and new AIDS cases from 506 to 108, a fall the paper says has been attributed primarily to expanded harm reduction, without saying by whom. Recorded drug-related deaths (deaths with a positive post-mortem test for an illegal drug, as the authors define this series in their later paper) went from a peak of 369 in 1999 and 280 in 2001 to about 150 a year in 2002–2004 and about 340 in 2008 (editors' readings of figures), while toxicological autopsies rose from 1,166 in 2002 to 2,805 in 2008; deaths that doctors certified as caused by drugs, a series that starts in 2001, went from about 76 in 2001 to about 9 in 2005 and about 20 in 2008 (editors' readings; Hughes & Stevens, 2012). Criminal drug arrests fell from over 14,000 people in 2000 to 5,000–5,500 a year, mostly because possession for personal use stopped counting as a crime: about 7,600 of the roughly 14,300 people arrested in 2000 were arrested for possession or use, and all police contacts for drug offences, crimes and administrative offences together, were about 10,500 to 12,000 a year after the reform against about 11,400 to 14,300 in 1998–2000 (editors' readings of a figure). The share of prisoners whose offences were drug-related fell from 44% in 1999 to 21% in 2008. Retail prices fell from 2001 (the peak year for heroin; cocaine and hash prices peaked in 2000), as measured from July 2001 by a different method; heroin and cocaine prices in 2008 were similar to those of 1998–1999. The authors state that it is impossible to say that any of these changes was the direct result of decriminalisation, and that expanded treatment and an ageing population of people who use heroin contributed. In a later critique of the two most publicised accounts, a report for the Cato Institute, a US libertarian think tank, that judged the reform a clear success and reports for an association for a drug-free Portugal (APLD) that judged it a clear failure, the same authors, who call themselves participants in the debate, found that each account rested on selected datasets and years, and argue that past-year use and doctor-certified deaths are better guides than lifetime use and toxicology-positive deaths (Hughes & Stevens, 2012; its erratum corrects only a remark on where one cited report could be found). The data end in 2008, with some series to 2009. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
lines.population: People in Portugal, in national statistics mostly for 1998–2008: people aged 15 to 64 in the national household surveys of 2001 and 2007; school students (ESPAD, aged 15 to 16, and other school surveys); estimated numbers of people with problem drug use and of people who inject drugs; people who use drugs newly diagnosed with HIV or AIDS; deaths recorded by the National Institute of Forensic Medicine (positive toxicology test) and the National Statistics Institute (certified by doctors, from 2001); people arrested or detected for drug offences; prisoners; with Spain and Italy for some indicators
lines.exposure: Decriminalisation of the acquisition, possession and use of all illegal drugs for personal use (up to ten days' supply), in force from 1 July 2001 under Law 30/2000: an administrative offence handled by regional dissuasion commissions instead of a crime; part of a national drug strategy that expanded prevention, harm reduction, treatment and social reintegration from May 1999
lines.comparator: Portugal before July 2001 (late 1990s to 2001, depending on the indicator; no adult survey before 2001 and no doctor-certified death series before 2001); Spain and Italy, which had made drug use an administrative offence in 1992 and 1990, for some indicators; no modelled counterfactual
lines.outcome: Reported drug use (lifetime, past year, past month) among adults and students; estimated problem and injecting drug use; new HIV and AIDS diagnoses among people who use drugs; drug-related deaths (toxicology-positive and doctor-certified); arrests and police contacts for drug offences; drug-related prisoners; retail prices; and what two publicised accounts claimed about these
