lines.magnitude: Hughes & Stevens (2010), Portugal, people aged 15–64: lifetime use of any illegal drug 7.8% (text; 7.6% in Table 1) in 2001 and 12.0% in 2007 (+4.4 points by Table 1); past-year 3.4% and 3.7% (+0.3); past-year cannabis 3.3% and 3.6%, cocaine 0.3% and 0.6%, heroin 0.2% and 0.3%, ecstasy 0.4% and 0.4%; Spain past-year cannabis 9.7% and 10.1%, cocaine 2.6% and 3.1%; Italy 6.2% and 14.6%, 1.1% and 2.2%. Students aged 15–16 (ESPAD), lifetime use of any illegal drug 8%, 12%, 18% and 14% in 1995, 1999, 2003 and 2007 (editors' reading). Problem drug use 7.6 (range 6.8–8.5) and 6.8 (6.2–7.4) per 1,000 aged 15–64 in 2000 and 2005; injecting 3.5 (2.3–4.6) and 2.0 (1.8–2.2); Italy, problem drug use 6.0 and 8.6 per 1,000 in 2001 and 2007. People in treatment 23,654 (1998) and 38,532 (2008). New HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs 907 (2000) and 267 (2008); AIDS 506 and 108. Recorded drug-related deaths 369 (1999); about 155, 152 and 157 in 2002–2004 and about 339 in 2008 (editors' readings of Figure 7); toxicological autopsies 1,166 (2002) and 2,805 (2008); deaths with opiates as the main substance 95% (1999) and 59% (2008). Criminal drug arrests over 14,000 (2000) and 5,000–5,500 a year after the reform; administrative detections about 6,000 a year; editors' readings of Figure 2: consumer offences about 7,600 of about 14,300 arrests in 2000; trafficking-type arrests about 4,500–6,300 a year in 1998–2000 and 5,200–5,600 in 2001–2008; all police contacts about 11,400–14,300 and 10,500–12,000 a year. Drug-related prisoners 44% (1999) and 21% (2008); prison density 119 (2001) and 101.5 (2005) per 100 places. Retail prices in euros per gram: heroin 38.50, 31.33, 49.72 and 50.27 (1998–2001) and 33.25 (2008); cocaine 45.63, 40.37, 60.31, 53.51 and 45.56. Hughes & Stevens (2012): toxicology-positive deaths (INML) 280 (2001), 216 (2006) and 314 (2007); doctor-certified drug deaths (INE) about 76 (2001), 34, 23, 20, 9 (2005), 12, 14 and 20 (2008) (editors' readings of Figure 4); adults' past-month use about 2.5% in 2001 and 2007; past-year use at 15–24 about 8.3% and 7.0%, at 25–34 about 4.9% and 7.0% (editors' readings of Figures 2 and 3); students' lifetime cannabis use (ESPAD) +60% around the reform, about 9.4% (1999) to 15.0% (2003), then about 13.0% (2007) (editors' readings of Figure 1). Neither paper gives intervals or statistical tests for these changes.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence (national before-and-after statistics, and a critique that compiles further national series) starts low; rated down two levels for risk of bias, it is very low, the floor. The claim concerns whether the law changed outcomes, so its relation is insufficient evidence; the trends are reported in it as descriptions of the national figures, not rated as a separate claim. Counted once: the 2012 critique is by the same authors, restates the 2010 comparison with Spain and Italy and uses the same toxicology-positive death series; its new data are the doctor-certified death series (INE, from 2001) and re-presented school and adult survey figures, which enter as second-hand national statistics, while its judgements of the two advocacy accounts enter as what it argues. Status contested: credible figures point both ways on whether drug problems eased after 2001 (lifetime use rose, past-year cocaine and heroin use rose by tenths of a point and toxicology-positive deaths returned near the 1999 peak by 2008, while past-year use overall barely changed and estimated injecting, HIV diagnoses among people who use drugs, drug-related prisoners and doctor-certified deaths fell), and the critique changes the reading of the death trend and shows that both publicised accounts rested on selected data, so the six-part debate box applies. The erratum to the 2012 paper (Drug Alcohol Rev 2012;31:727, 10.1111/j.1465-3362.2012.00462.x), now read, corrects only the statement that a cited report of the US Office of National Drug Control Policy could not be found on that office's website (p. 111); nothing used here changes. Neither paper has a conflict-of-interest statement; the authors had studied the reform for years, partly in collaboration with the agency that ran it, and wrote one of the accounts in the debate.

lines.q: What happened after Portugal decriminalised all drugs?
lines.short: Mixed. Adults who'd ever tried a drug went from 8 to 12 in 100, but use in the last year barely moved. New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.
lines.but: Treatment and other help grew too, starting in 1999, so these figures can't show what the law alone did.
how: In 2001, having any drug for your own use became an offence handled by regional panels, not a crime. Mostly for that reason, crime arrests for drugs fell from over 14,000 to 5,000–5,500 a year.
Adults who had ever tried an illegal drug rose from about 8 to 12 in 100 (2001 to 2007); past-year use barely changed.
New HIV cases in people who use drugs fell from 907 (2000) to 267 (2008). The paper says this has been credited mainly to more harm reduction services, without saying by whom.
Deaths doctors judged drug-caused fell from about 76 to 20 (2001 to 2008). Deaths with drugs found fell, then rose as testing more than doubled.
lines.q_on_site_now: What happened after Portugal decriminalised all drugs?

lines.statement: In British Columbia in 2019, take-home testing by people who use drugs (strips from ten harm-reduction sites, used at home on 55 in 100 result sheets, in alleys and streets on 22 and at supervised consumption or overdose prevention sites on 29, more than one setting possible; 218 people returning 336 result sheets) compared with on-site testing of other samples by trained staff at the same sites in the same four months was associated with a similar share of fentanyl-positive results for opioid samples and a much larger share for stimulant samples. Opioids: 994 of 1105 take-home results positive (90.0%) against 591 of 663 on site (89.1%), a difference of 0.8 percentage points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9) within the pre-set equivalence margin of ±5 points. Crystal methamphetamine: 73 of 265 (27.6% as printed) against 5 of 97 (5.2%); cocaine: 16 of 93 (17.2%) against 1 of 92 (1.1%); the study was not powered for these. By design no sample was tested both ways, and nothing was confirmed in a laboratory, so these are shares of positive results, not accuracy; the authors nonetheless conclude that people can use the strips accurately with minimal training, and think the stimulant excess mostly reflects false positives from how samples were prepared, which was not tested (Klaire et al., 2022). Results were self-reported, about 6 in 10 sheets were filled in from memory at return (by the paper's Table 3; its text gives the reverse), the number of kits handed out and not returned is unknown, and similar shares near 90% can hide reading errors in both directions. A scoping review relays from three US syringe services programme studies that 3% to almost 34% of people had difficulty interpreting results and that some believed the line's strength showed how strong the fentanyl was (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand; its figure of positives five times more frequent at home is this same study, as its complete reference list confirms, and holds only for crystal methamphetamine); a 2018 commentary relays a preliminary study, with design and testers not stated, in which 7 of 70 samples gave erroneous or invalid results (McGowan et al., 2018, second-hand); and in a laboratory study of a colour kit, two testers new to it misread known drugs in both directions (Murray et al., 2003). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: People using ten harm-reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, April to July 2019, who took home fentanyl test strips and returned results (218 people, 336 sheets, 1680 strip results)
lines.exposure: Fentanyl test strips used and read by the person wherever they chose to test, after brief peer training
lines.comparator: On-site testing of other samples with the same strips by trained staff at the same sites in the same months (852 samples)
lines.outcome: Share of fentanyl-positive strip results, by the drug the sample was expected to be
lines.magnitude: Opioids: take-home 994/1105 (90.0%) against on-site 591/663 (89.1%); difference 0.8 points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9), equivalent within ±5 (p = 0.00275). Crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6% as printed; 27.5% by the counts, editors' calculation) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 (14.8 to 30.1); cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), difference 16.1 (7.1 to 25.1). Settings of take-home use (sheets, more than one possible): home 184 (54.8%), alleys and streets 74 (22.0%), supervised sites 97 (28.9%). Second-hand: difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34% (Kutscher et al., citing Peiper et al., 2019, Tilhou et al., 2022, and Park et al., 2021); its 'five times more frequent at home' matches this study's crystal methamphetamine figures only (27.6% against 5.2%, 5.3-fold; cocaine about 16-fold; opioids equal; editors' calculation); 7 of 70 erroneous or invalid results in a preliminary study (McGowan et al.).
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each rate it down, to the floor of very low. Rated as worded: agreement of shares of positive results between people using take-home strips and staff testing on site, not the accuracy of home testing, which no study read measured; whether home testing changes behaviour is a separate question. Status single study: the review's 'five times' figure is the same study (its reference 66, listed again as 92, is Klaire et al., 2022, by the review's Appendix 1), and Murray et al. concerns a colour kit in a laboratory and only qualifies.

lines.q: Do take-home fentanyl strips match what trained staff find?
lines.short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often: 28 in 100 meth samples, against 5 in 100 tested by staff.
lines.but: The two groups tested different samples, and no lab checked which results were right.
how: In 2019, people took strips from ten health sites and used them at home a little over half the time. Staff tested other samples at the sites.
Opioids: 90 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, and 89 in 100 on site.
Crystal meth: 28 in 100 take-home results showed fentanyl, against 5 in 100 on site; cocaine, 17 against 1. The authors think most extra positives were false, but didn't test it.
People told the study their own results, often from memory.
lines.q_on_site_now: Do results with take-home strips match testing by trained staff?

lines.statement: In adults with major depression, most of them with depression that had not responded to earlier antidepressants and, in the three trials read, taken off their psychiatric medicines, one 40-minute infusion of racemic ketamine into a vein, given by clinicians in randomized trials (trial conditions: 0.5 mg per kg of body weight), compared with an infusion of salt water (saline) or of midazolam, a sedative chosen as an active placebo so that people could less easily tell which infusion they had, is associated with lower clinician-rated depression scores within hours, largest at about one day, with most responses fading within weeks. In the first small trial (Berman et al., 2000; Connecticut, USA; 9 people, 7 of whom had both infusion days of a crossover), depression scores (25-item Hamilton scale) fell by 14 points (SD 10) within 72 hours after ketamine and by 0 (SD 12) after saline; 4 of 8 people had their score fall by half or more within 3 days after ketamine, against 1 of 8 after saline, a difference that was not statistically significant; by the authors' account mood was back near its starting level 1 to 2 weeks after the infusion, an observation outside the trial's rating schedule, and patients could readily tell the two infusions apart, which, the authors write, may have biased their reporting. In a crossover trial at the US National Institute of Mental Health (Zarate et al., 2006; November 2004 to September 2005; 18 inpatients with recurrent major depression without psychosis who had failed at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials, 5.7 lifetime trials on average; 17 given ketamine and 14 saline, 13 both; funded by the Institute's intramural programme, with no conflict statement printed), Hamilton scores were lower after ketamine than after saline from 110 minutes to day 7 in the analysis of the 13 who had both infusions (standardized difference 1.46, 95% CI 0.91 to 2.01, at 24 hours and 0.68, 0.13 to 1.23, at 1 week) and from 80 minutes to day 7 in an analysis of the first infusion only (18 people compared between groups). Counting everyone with data, 12 of 17 (71 in 100) had their score fall by half or more the day after ketamine, against 0 of 14 after saline; 5 of 17 reached remission (a score of 7 or less) against none; and 6 of 17 (35 in 100) kept the response for at least a week, 2 of them for at least 2 weeks; about half of those given ketamine had responded by 110 minutes (editors' reading of a figure). After correction for repeated testing only the day-1 difference in responders stayed significant, and remission did not differ significantly at any time; the trial stopped at 18 of a planned 22 after an interim analysis, and people given ketamine first began their saline week less depressed (Hamilton 17.2 against 24.9), a carry-over; its authors write that ketamine's short-lived perceptual effects could have affected the blind and biased patients' reporting. In a two-site trial with parallel groups (Murrough et al., 2013; Baylor College of Medicine and Mount Sinai, New York, November 2010 to August 2012; 73 medication-free adults who had failed at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials, randomized 2 to 1, 72 analysed: 47 given ketamine and 25 midazolam; raters kept away from the infusion day), depression scores 24 hours after the infusion, the primary outcome, were 7.95 points lower after ketamine on the 0-to-60 MADRS (95% CI 3.20 to 12.71; means 14.77 against 22.72), and 30 of 47 (64 in 100) against 7 of 25 (28 in 100) had their score fall by half or more, a difference of 36 percentage points (95% CI 12 to 54, editors' calculation; the printed odds ratio of 2.18 is smaller than these counts give, 4.5). Over days 1 to 7 ketamine scores stayed lower on average (16.93 against 23.19), but at day 7 depression scores and response rates no longer differed significantly in the authors' analysis adjusted for site and baseline. At day 7, 21 people given ketamine and 4 given midazolam still met the response criterion and chose to continue in the study: 21 of 47 (45 in 100) against 4 of 25 (16 in 100), counting everyone analysed and treating anyone not rated that day as not responding (editors' arithmetic, used here because the article prints these group sizes and no day-7 denominators); the article's bars (about 46% and 18%) fit 21 of 46 and 4 of 22, the people rated that day. Among those 21 ketamine responders, followed for up to 4 more weeks, the share still without relapse fell to about 4 in 10 by about the 17th day of follow-up (editors' reading of a figure; no numbers are printed). Dissociation (feeling outside one's body, time running slower or faster) was significant in 8 of 47 after ketamine and resolved within 2 hours, and blurred vision on the infusion day was reported by 20 of 47 against 2 of 25; the authors say no control for ketamine is perfect and that dissociation was more frequent with ketamine, and none of the three trials reports asking patients or raters which infusion they thought they had. The 2013 trial was funded by the US National Institutes of Health, the Department of Veterans Affairs, a NARSAD award and the Brown Foundation; one author and the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai were named on a use-patent application of ketamine for depression, another author was named as an inventor on a pending use patent and had given up any royalties, and several authors reported research support or fees from drug companies. A meta-analysis of 49 randomized trials (3299 participants) of racemic ketamine or esketamine against control conditions, searched to April 2023 (Nikolin et al., 2023; no funding; one author, the first author of the 2006 trial, is co-inventor on patents for ketamine in depression, with rights assigned to the US government and a share of royalties), gives no estimate for the intravenous route alone: its high-dose racemic category (0.5 mg/kg into a vein, or a dose judged equivalent by another route) includes 25 trials with a racemic arm into a vein at 0.5 mg/kg or more, among them the three above (editors' count from its table: 14 with saline, 10 with midazolam and 1 with remifentanil as control; each with fewer than 100 participants, median 30), and some arms given by other routes. For this category, from 4 hours to 3 days after a first or single dose, the standardized difference in depression scores against control was −0.73 (95% CI −0.91 to −0.56), which the authors call large, the odds ratio for response 5.35 (3.48 to 8.22) and for remission 2.97 (1.77 to 4.99), with substantial heterogeneity in the model for scores (I² 60.5% across all categories); its pooled estimates for this category plotted by time are about −0.6 at 4 hours, −0.9 at day 1 and −0.6 at day 3 (editors' reading of a figure), and the authors read their model's curved time term as a fall in depression scores that peaks about one day after the dose and then returns towards baseline. The review pooled no data from single doses beyond 3 days, its later windows concerning repeated courses. Its funnel-plot analysis suggested missing null results at 4 hours, 1 day and 3 days after a first dose, which would make the early effect look larger, an asymmetry the authors say may instead reflect a shift from small saline-controlled pilot trials to larger trials with better-blinded controls; they also name compromised blinding in crossover trials as a limitation. Certainty: low. Status: replicated by the same team.
lines.population: Adults with major depression in randomized trials, mostly treatment-resistant: 9 medication-free adults with a major depressive episode (8 unipolar, 1 bipolar) in Connecticut, USA, 7 of whom had both infusion days (Berman et al., 2000); 18 medication-free inpatients with recurrent major depression without psychosis who had failed at least 2 adequate antidepressant trials, at the US National Institute of Mental Health, 2004 to 2005 (Zarate et al., 2006); 73 medication-free adults aged 21 to 80 who had failed at least 3 adequate antidepressant trials, at Baylor College of Medicine and Mount Sinai, 2010 to 2012, 72 analysed (Murrough et al., 2013); and the participants of 49 randomized trials of racemic ketamine or esketamine to April 2023 (3299 participants; 33 trials in treatment-resistant samples; including trials in bipolar depression, adolescents and suicidal ideation), 25 of which had an arm of racemic ketamine into a vein at 0.5 mg/kg or more (Nikolin et al., 2023)
lines.exposure: One 40-minute intravenous infusion of racemic ketamine given by clinicians in trials (trial conditions: 0.5 mg per kg of body weight; given by an anaesthesiologist in the 2006 trial); in the review, its high-dose racemic category (0.5 mg/kg into a vein, or a dose it judged equivalent by another route), from 4 hours to 3 days after a first or single dose
lines.comparator: An infusion of salt water (saline) on another day, in random order (crossover: Berman et al., 2000; Zarate et al., 2006); an infusion of midazolam, a short-acting sedative chosen as an active placebo to mimic ketamine's sedation and disorientation so that people could less easily tell which they had (parallel groups, randomized 2 to 1: Murrough et al., 2013; trial conditions 0.045 mg per kg over 40 minutes); in the review, the trials' control arms (in the 25 trials with an intravenous high-dose racemic arm, saline in 14, midazolam in 10 and remifentanil in 1; editors' count)
lines.outcome: Clinician-rated depression (Hamilton scale, MADRS) from 40 minutes to 7 days after the infusion; response (a fall of 50% or more) and remission; time to relapse in day-7 responders (Murrough et al., 2013); in the review, the standardized mean difference in depression scores and odds ratios for response and remission from 4 hours to 3 days after a first or single dose
lines.magnitude: Berman et al. (2000), 7 completers: HDRS change within 72 hours −14 (SD 10) after ketamine against 0 (SD 12) after saline; condition × time F = 3.97, df 5,30, p = .02; response 4 of 8 against 1 of 8 (Fisher p > .05; editors' two-sided 0.28). Zarate et al. (2006): completers (13), ketamine better than saline from 110 minutes to day 7, d 1.46 (95% CI 0.91 to 2.01) at 24 hours and 0.68 (0.13 to 1.23) at 1 week (drug F(1,203) = 58.24, drug × time F(8,203) = 4.15, P < .001); first infusion only (18), drug F(1,16) = 10.44, P = .005, lower from 80 minutes to day 7; intent to treat, response on day 1 12/17 (71%) against 0/14, remission 5/17 (29%) against 0/14, response kept at least 1 week 6/17 (35%), at least 2 weeks 2/17; Figure 3A (editors' reading) ketamine response about 0.12, 0.35, 0.53 and 0.56 at 40, 80, 110 and 230 minutes, 0.71, 0.59 and 0.53 on days 1 to 3 and 0.35 on day 7. Murrough et al. (2013): MADRS at 24 hours 14.77 against 22.72, adjusted difference 7.95 (3.20 to 12.71), d 0.81; response 30/47 (64%) against 7/25 (28%), risk difference 35.8 percentage points (11.6 to 54.2; Newcombe, editors' calculation), printed odds ratio 2.18 (1.21 to 4.14) against a crude 4.54 from the counts (editors'), number needed to treat 2.8; QIDS-SR16 lower by 3.40 (0.78 to 6.01); days 1 to 7 mean MADRS 16.93 against 23.19 (treatment F = 5.93, P ≤ 0.02; treatment × time F = 0.31); day 7 not significant (adjusted); responders still continuing at day 7, 21 ketamine and 4 midazolam: 21/47 (44.7%) against 4/25 (16.0%) over the groups analysed, or 21/46 (45.7%) against 4/22 (18.2%) as Figure 2's bars fit (measured at 45.8% and 18.4%, editors'); relapse-free among the 21 ketamine day-7 responders about 0.79, 0.74, 0.68, 0.63 and 0.42 at about days 3, 7, 10, 14 and 17 of follow-up (editors' reading of Figure 3); dissociation 8/47 (17%); blurred vision on the infusion day 20/47 (43%) against 2/25 (8%). Nikolin et al. (2023), high-dose racemic category, 4 hours to 3 days after a first or single dose: SMD −0.73 (−0.91 to −0.56), I² 60.5% for the whole model (k = 43); response OR 5.35 (3.48 to 8.22), k = 37, I² 44.0%; remission OR 2.97 (1.77 to 4.99), k = 25, I² 9.9%; quadratic time 0.81 (0.10 to 1.52), p = 0.025; Fig. 2 aggregates (editors' reading) about −0.61 at 4 hours, −0.87 at day 1 and −0.61 at day 3.
lines.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high: three randomized trials read in full and a meta-analysis of 49 randomized trials that includes all three. Down one level for risk of bias (outcomes that rest on what patients report, with a drug whose effects patients notice, no check of what anyone guessed, and carry-over and early stopping in the crossover trials) and one for publication bias (the review's own analysis suggests missing null results in exactly the 4-hour to 3-day window): low. Rated as worded: lower depression scores within hours, largest at about a day, after one 40-minute infusion under trial conditions against saline or midazolam, with the fading given as each trial reports it; the claim does not say how large the effect is apart from expectation, how long it lasts beyond these trials' follow-up, or that ketamine works better than other treatments. 'Is associated with' because the certainty is low (METHODS §6.1), although the comparisons are randomized. Status replicated by the same team (METHODS §6.4): the three trials read share an author (Dennis S. Charney is an author of all three), and the review, which pools 25 trials with an intravenous arm of this kind from many groups, prints only pooled estimates, not each trial's direction (its forest plots are in an appendix not read), so independent replication is not counted from it; the review contains the three trials and its authors include the first author of the 2006 trial, so it is one body of evidence with them, not a separate confirmation. Day 7 in the 2013 trial: the counts 21 and 4 are printed without day-7 denominators; 21 of 47 against 4 of 25 (the groups as analysed, anyone not rated that day counted as not responding) is used in the plain lines because it rests only on printed numbers, while the bars fit 21 of 46 and 4 of 22 (the people rated that day), and both are given. Editors' calculations, for the second reader: the 2013 risk difference (Newcombe) and crude odds ratio, the day-7 shares, the 2000 trial's two-sided Fisher p, the count of intravenous trials in the review's table, and the readings of Figure 3A (2006), Figures 2 and 3 (2013) and Fig. 2 (review). Not used: the review's estimates for repeated courses and after a course (which include racemic ketamine given under the skin, by nose and by mouth), its dose and formulation comparisons, its esketamine estimates and its conclusion that higher doses work better, which its own estimates do not bear out (card sc_nikolin_2023); side effects are covered by another answer on the page. Funding as printed: the 2000 trial by foundation, Veterans Affairs and state grants; the 2006 trial by the NIMH intramural programme; the 2013 trial by the NIH, Veterans Affairs and foundations, with patent filings for ketamine in depression and industry ties among its authors; the review unfunded, with one author a co-inventor on ketamine patents and two with Janssen ties. The review's study card is still in data/study-cards/_incoming/ketamine/, so the claim cannot be merged until the card is.

lines.q: Can a ketamine drip lift depression within hours, and for how long?
lines.short: It can, within hours. A day after one drip, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 after a sedative drip. For most, it faded within weeks.
lines.but: People can often tell they got ketamine, which may make the lift look bigger.
how: In a 2006 trial, 12 of 17 people were much better a day after a ketamine drip. After a salt-water drip, none of 14 were.
In a 2013 trial, 72 people got ketamine or a sedative, picked to make it hard to guess which. Other medicines had failed them.
Pooled trials show the gap is biggest about a day after a ketamine drip. In the 2013 trial, it was not clear by a week.
Two of the 2013 trial's authors were named on patent applications for ketamine in depression. One gave up any share of the money.
lines.q_on_site_now: Can a ketamine drip lift depression within hours, and for how long?

lines.statement: Whether the phase 3 trials show that MDMA itself, given within an intensive therapy, is an effective and acceptably safe treatment for PTSD is contested, and the sources read here cannot settle it. Two randomized trials from one sponsor (MAPP1, 90 adults; MAPP2, 104) found larger falls in PTSD symptom scores with MDMA than with placebo plus the same therapy at 18 weeks (11.9 and 8.9 CAPS-5 points; see the efficacy claim in section 12) and no serious adverse events on MDMA during treatment. Against this, in MAPP2, the only trial that asked, most participants identified their group, and neither trial reports a measure of expectancy; the comparator was placebo, not a trauma-focused psychotherapy; the trial reports give no outcome after 18 weeks, and the only later data, from an observational follow-up visit, were judged by the FDA not designed to evaluate durability (the sponsor presents them as evidence of durability); expected drug effects were not solicited as adverse events (MAPP1) and, the FDA reports, positive drug effects went unrecorded across the programme, against its advice of 2017; in 2024 the US regulator declined approval (as reported) after its advisory committee voted 9 to 2 that the data did not show effectiveness and 10 to 1 that the benefits did not outweigh the risks, citing functional unblinding and expectation bias (the committee's minutes); and three analyses from the sponsor's phase 2 programme, including the one that set out the rationale for the phase 3 trials, were retracted because the authors had not disclosed protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at one site, or removed that site's data, and had not fully declared competing interests (the retraction notices). The regulator's briefing document and the committee's minutes were read; its decision letter was not. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
lines.population: Adults with PTSD considered for MDMA-assisted therapy
lines.exposure: MDMA in three sessions within a manualized therapy
lines.comparator: The same therapy with placebo; trauma-focused psychotherapy; the course of PTSD after treatment ends
lines.outcome: PTSD symptoms beyond the trial period and harms in clinical use attributable to MDMA itself
lines.magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of MDMA separate from expectancy, or beyond 18 weeks: the only later data, an observational visit attended by 137 of 195 randomized, cannot separate a lasting effect from self-selection, unblinding and interim treatments (FDA). The trials' between-group differences at 18 weeks are 11.9 (95% CI 6.3 to 17.4) and 8.9 (4.1 to 13.7) CAPS-5 points; 94% and 75% of MAPP2 participants identified their allocation. Advisory committee votes: yes 2, no 9 on effectiveness; yes 1, no 10 on benefit-risk.
lines.reasoning: Rated for the question as posed, which goes beyond what the trials measured. Starting high (randomized trials). Risk of bias, two levels, as in the efficacy claim: unblinding (measured in MAPP2, not assessed in MAPP1) with a participant-reported outcome and no reported measure of expectancy, a bias shared by both trials and of unknown size against differences of comparable order. Indirectness, one level: the question concerns MDMA's own contribution, durability beyond 18 weeks, comparison with existing psychotherapy and harms in clinical use, none of which the trials measured directly. The short-term comparison with placebo plus the same therapy is rated separately (low, section 12), as is the rise in common adverse events (moderate, section 12). Contested (METHODS §6.4): credible published critiques and the 2024 regulatory events change the interpretation of the trials.

lines.q: Do the MDMA therapy trials hold up?
lines.short: It's not settled. Two trials found PTSD eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill, but can't show how much was the drug itself, or for how long.
lines.but: One sponsor ran both trials, and in the one that asked, most people knew their pill.
how: Two trials found PTSD eased more with MDMA and therapy than with a dummy pill and the same therapy. Neither tested MDMA against usual talking therapy.
But in the second trial most people could tell which pill they had, and neither trial reports measuring what they expected.
The company's own later check found the gap lasted. The regulator said it wasn't built to show that. About 3 in 10 weren't checked, and some knew their pill.
In 2024 the US regulator said no, after its advisers voted 9 to 2 that it wasn't shown to work. Three earlier studies were withdrawn for not disclosing rule-breaking at one site.
lines.q_on_site_now: Do the MDMA therapy trials hold up?

lines.statement: In one randomized online experiment with UK adults, details in a simulated news report of a drug death changed how much stigma readers said they felt towards the person who died, by small to moderate amounts, but hardly changed their stated support for harm-reduction policies. In June 2022, 1,248 adults on a UK online research panel (Prolific; mean age 45.7, 51.0% women) were each randomly assigned to read one of eight versions of a BBC-style news story about an inquest, adapted from a real BBC report of an ecstasy death in 2019; the versions differed in the person's gender (Jane or John), age together with use history (21 and had used the drug 'once or twice', or 43 and had used it regularly for 15 years) and drug (ecstasy or heroin). Stigma towards the person, on a new nine-item measure of blame, anger, pity, responsibility, control and wish for distance (range 9 to 81), was higher when the person was a man (mean 45.6 against 43.4 for a woman), when the person was older with long use (46.7 against 42.3) and when the drug was heroin (46.9 against 42.1): about 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4 standard deviations (editors' calculation), with the eight versions ranging from 38.6 (young woman, ecstasy) to 50.1 (older man, heroin). Support for six harm-reduction policies (such as drug checking, drug consumption rooms, take-home naloxone and opioid agonist treatment; range 6 to 30) was slightly higher after the older person's story (about 23.6 against 23.0, editors' calculation from the condition means, about 0.1 standard deviation; the paper prints the two means in reverse order), a difference seen in the ecstasy stories only (about 23.9 against 22.7, with none in the heroin stories, editors' calculation), and did not differ by drug or by gender. In exploratory, non-randomized analyses of 868 participants, stronger belief in a just world, less perspective-taking and more general stigma towards people with drug problems went with more stigma towards the person, and having seen media coverage of a family affected by a drug death went with less (Sumnall et al., 2023). The study was not registered in advance, the stigma measure was new, the panel was matched to the UK population on sex, age and ethnicity only and over-represented people with degrees and people who prefer left-wing parties, the outcomes were self-reports measured once straight after one written story, and 'older' cannot be separated from 'longer use'. How real news coverage affects behaviour, policy or the people affected was not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
lines.population: UK adults on an online research panel (Prolific), June 2022; 1,248 randomized (mean age 45.7, 51.0% women; matched to the UK on sex, age and ethnicity)
lines.exposure: Reading a simulated news report of a drug death in which the person who died was a man, was 43 with 15 years of regular use, or died after heroin
lines.comparator: Versions of the same report in which the person was a woman, was 21 and had used the drug once or twice, or died after ecstasy (factorial randomization)
lines.outcome: Self-reported stigma towards the person depicted (new nine-item measure) and stated support for six harm-reduction policies, measured once, straight after reading
lines.magnitude: Sumnall et al. (2023), 2 × 2 × 2 factorial, n = 1,248 (degrees of freedom imply 1,238 analysed). Stigma (9–81): man 45.6 (SD 12.1) against woman 43.4 (12.6), F(1,1230) = 11.1, p < .001; older with 15 years' use 46.7 (11.8) against younger, used once or twice, 42.3 (12.7), F = 40.5, p < .001; heroin 46.9 (11.5) against ecstasy 42.1 (12.8), F = 50.1, p < .001; editors' d about 0.18, 0.36 and 0.39; condition means 38.6 to 50.1. Harm-reduction support (6–30): age, F = 4.5, p = .035 (older about 23.6 against younger 23.0, editors' calculation; d about 0.12); in the ecstasy stories about 23.9 against 22.7 and in the heroin stories 23.3 against 23.3 (editors' calculation from Table 1); the F = 4.8, p = .029 printed with the ecstasy comparison is more consistent with an interaction in an approximate reconstruction (age-by-drug F about 5.4; within-ecstasy age F about 10.1), but rounded Table 1 summaries cover 1,248 assigned participants while the residual degrees of freedom imply 1,238 analysed under the full eight-cell model, so the exact test identity remains unresolved (editors’ conditional calculation); gender F = .0, p = .802; drug F = .0, p = .922. Exploratory regression (868 participants, editors' calculation from degrees of freedom): story factors R² = .068, final model R² = .569.
lines.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: low. The verb 'increases' rests on random assignment within the experiment and applies to stigma towards the depicted person; for support for harm-reduction policies the claim reports a very small difference by age with use history and no difference by drug or gender. The participant-trait associations come from non-randomized regressions on 868 participants and are reported as associations. Status single study; the authors report no earlier experiment on news depictions of drug deaths.

lines.q: Does how the news describes a drug death change what readers think?
lines.short: Yes, somewhat. Readers judged the person who died more harshly when the story said heroin, not ecstasy, or an older person with years of use.
lines.but: Readers saw one made-up story and answered straight away; nobody checked what they did later.
how: In 2022, 1,248 adults in the UK each read one made-up news story about a drug death, with the details chosen at random.
Readers judged the person more harshly when the person was a man, was older and had used the drug for years, or had taken heroin rather than ecstasy. The differences were small to moderate.
Support for services that reduce harm, such as drug checking, barely changed.
The study could not tell the effect of age apart from the effect of using the drug for longer.
lines.q_on_site_now: Does how the news describes a drug death change what readers think?

lines.statement: In people with alcohol or drug problems followed for between about a year and several decades, a large share no longer met the criteria for the problem at a later interview, but how many depends on who was counted (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, or people who had already recovered), on how a problem, recovery ('remission') and treatment were defined, and on the length of the time window; how many recovered without treatment was measured only in studies of alcohol problems. Of 451 men interviewed from a random sample of 470 US Army enlisted men who returned from Vietnam in September 1971 (interviews 8 to 12 months after return), 43% had used narcotics there (about a third of the men had tried heroin) and 20% reported having been dependent on narcotics there (21% by the study's own criteria for dependence), against 10% who had used narcotics and 0.7% who reported dependence (1% by the criteria) since their return; of 134 men from the study's two samples who were still dependent when they left Vietnam, 50% used narcotics again after return and 14% were dependent again (the table's numbers add up to both samples together, with no weighting stated). The authors give a remission rate of 95% without saying which sample it describes; their figure, read approximately, shows that of the men first dependent in Vietnam, about 2% of 90 in the general sample and about 7% of 341 in a second sample (selected on a urine test at departure positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates) were dependent again. Remission there meant not being dependent again within about a year; many of the men counted as remitted still used narcotics, and a period of more-than-weekly narcotic use was more common after return than before Vietnam (3% against under 0.5%); men whose urine was positive at departure were to be held for detoxification and treatment, but how many men received drug treatment, before or after return, is not reported; and the authors leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change from Vietnam to home explains the remission (Robins et al., 1975). In a US national survey of adults interviewed in 2001–2002 and again about three years later (34,653 re-interviewed), 422 of the 1,172 people who had met the criteria for alcohol dependence in the year before the first interview met them again in the year before the second (36%), so about 64% did not (1,172 = 422 + 750, an editors' sum; both shares are editors' calculations from unweighted counts in a survey that over-sampled young adults and Black and Hispanic people, so they are not national estimates); in the paper's own weighted analysis, persistence was 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at ages 43–52. Not meeting the full criteria can include people with one or two symptoms left, and treatment between the interviews is not reported (Vergés et al., 2012). A meta-analysis of 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders, published 2000–2015 and mostly from the US (20 cohorts followed for 3 to 50 years, mean 17, 15 of them recruited through treatment, and one national survey that estimated remission over a lifetime), found 54% (95% CI 42% to 66%) of the people followed to the end in remission at the last follow-up, and 35% (25% to 46%) of everyone enrolled when deaths and people lost to follow-up were counted as not remitted; without the lifetime survey, about 50% (editors' recalculation) and 31%. Among the people followed to the end, single studies ranged from about 20% to 96%, the top value being the lifetime survey, and this rate, unlike the rate among everyone enrolled, was higher in cohorts followed longer and in cohorts that kept fewer of their participants. For treatment, the review compared cohorts only by whether people were in treatment when they entered, which cannot show who recovered without treatment: 51% with treatment at entry against 62% without (p 0.42), the six without including the lifetime survey (about 49% without it, editors' recalculation). Treatment during follow-up was not analysed, the pooled figures mix very different follow-up times and so describe no particular time point, the review reports no appraisal of its cohorts, and its authors read the results as showing that for many people these disorders are long-lasting (Fleury et al., 2016). For alcohol problems, a review of 124 estimates of recovery without treatment from 27 published studies (1976–2018, 24 of them North American; 71 of the estimates, the lowest among them, calculated by the reviewers from the studies' data) found figures from 2.7% to 98.3%, largely because the studies counted different things: among people already recovered, the share never treated (78% in two Canadian population surveys when recovery included moderate drinking, 56% and 66% when it meant not drinking); among people with an alcohol problem who stayed untreated, the share who recovered (in the US national survey of 2001–2002, 12.4% when recovery meant not drinking and 32.6% when moderate drinking also counted; in a Dutch survey, 78% of people with an alcohol use disorder who stayed untreated for three years were in remission at follow-up, against 40% of those whose disorder was moderate or severe; in one US cohort of people who had had no treatment beyond a single detoxification or a visit to an information and referral centre, 36.0% were in remission at both the 1- and 3-year follow-ups, and 14.0% when it also had to hold 16 years later); and among everyone with an alcohol problem, the share who recovered without treatment, which gave the lowest figures (2.7% to 63.6% in the nine studies that allowed all three counts). Most studies used a window of about one year, the review did not appraise the studies, and these figures are second-hand (Mellor et al., 2019). So a high share of never-treated people among those who recovered and a much lower share of everyone with a problem recovering without treatment in a year can both be right. No source read here measured recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol; for the Vietnam veterans, how many were treated is not reported. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: US Army enlisted men returning from Vietnam in September 1971, interviewed 8 to 12 months later (451 in a random general sample; 898 in both samples) (Robins et al., 1975); US adults in a national household survey interviewed in 2001–2002 and 2004–2005 (34,653 re-interviewed; 1,172 of them with past-year alcohol dependence at the first interview, an editors' sum) (Vergés et al., 2012); 21 studies of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders published 2000–2015 (20 cohorts, 15 recruited through treatment, and one national survey's lifetime estimate) (Fleury et al., 2016); 27 studies of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018, mostly North American (Mellor et al., 2019)
lines.exposure: Having had an alcohol or drug problem (narcotic dependence in Vietnam, self-reported or by the study's own criteria; DSM-IV alcohol dependence; substance use disorders as each cohort diagnosed them; alcohol problems as each study defined them), with or without treatment as each study defined it
lines.comparator: None (descriptive); the same people's earlier status; in the alcohol review, three different denominators (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, people already recovered)
lines.outcome: No longer meeting the criteria for the problem (remission) at a later interview or at the last follow-up, as each study defined it (not dependent again within about a year; not meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the year before an interview about three years later; at least six months without meeting criteria; abstinence or moderate drinking), and the share of it without treatment
lines.magnitude: Robins et al. (1975), general sample N=451, before / in / since Vietnam: narcotic use 11% / 43% / 10%; dependence self-reported 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%. Still dependent at departure (both samples pooled, no weighting stated, n=134): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% dependent again. A period of more-than-weekly narcotic use since return 3% vs under 0.5% before service. Men first dependent in Vietnam dependent again 8–10 months after return (Figure, approximate): about 2% (general sample, N=90) and about 7% (urine-positive sample, N=341). Stated remission rate 95% (no denominator). Vergés et al. (2012), NESARC 2001–2002 to 2004–2005: 422 of 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence (36%) dependent again about three years later, about 64% (750) not (1,172 = 422 + 750, and both shares are editors' calculations, unweighted); weighted persistence 32.4% (ages 21–23) and 44.5% (43–52). Fleury et al. (2016), 21 studies (20 cohorts, follow-up 3–50 years, and one lifetime survey estimate entered as 95.7%): standard remission 54.4% (95% CI 42.1–66.2), studies 19.6–95.7%, I² 99.4%; conservative 35.0% (25.2–46.4), I² 99.5%; without the lifetime survey, standard about 50.1% (42.5–57.6; editors' recalculation from Fig. 4, matching the lowest printed leave-one-out value) and conservative 30.9% (26.1–36.1, printed); treatment at baseline 51.1% vs not 62.4% (standard rate, p 0.421; about 48–49% for the five cohorts without treatment at baseline other than the lifetime survey, editors' recalculation; the printed conservative-rate subgroups could not be rebuilt from Fig. 4); standard rate higher with longer follow-up (B 0.046 per year, p 0.004) and lower retention (p 0.016), neither for the conservative rate. Mellor et al. (2019), alcohol, 124 estimates (71 calculated by the reviewers): 2.7% to 98.3%; nine studies with all three methods: all people with a problem 2.7–63.6%, untreated people 6.5–77.9%, remitted people 4.3–94.2% (6.4% with Table 3's values) (unweighted medians 12.4, 38.9 and 43.9, not rates); 78% of remitted people untreated (two Canadian surveys; abstinence or moderate drinking; 56.0% and 65.7% with abstinence only); 12.4% vs 32.6% of untreated people remitted (abstinence vs abstinence or moderate drinking; NESARC); 78% vs 40% of people untreated for three years in remission (any vs moderate or severe disorder; Netherlands); 36.0% vs 14.0% (remission at both 1 and 3 years vs also at 16 years; the 14.0% a reviewers' calculation; a US cohort).
lines.reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low and is rated as a description of the samples. Down one for risk of bias, because the part of the question about recovery without treatment rests on second-hand, unappraised estimates (and on a meta-analysis of unappraised, mostly treatment-recruited cohorts): very low. A lenient reading would rate the Vietnam and national-survey figures alone (primary data from a near-complete random sample and a weighted national survey) as low for the narrower statement that many people no longer meet the criteria within one to three years; the rating is set by the weakest necessary link. Not upgraded (descriptive). Status replicated: the direction holds in independent samples (Vietnam veterans; the US national survey; the cohorts pooled by Fleury et al.), but the US national survey appears in four places (Vergés et al.; two of the studies pooled by Fleury et al., the lifetime estimate and Moss et al., 2010, a general-population sample from the same survey followed for three years; and Dawson et al. in Mellor et al.), which are not counted as independent of each other. Not used: the 95% remission rate as a figure (no stated denominator), Fleury et al.'s annual remission rates (inconsistent with its pooled proportions), its 14 years of use before remission (not derivable from its table) and its conservative-rate comparison by treatment at entry (not reproducible from its study values), and Mellor et al.'s medians as rates (card reporting issues). The comparison of cohorts by treatment at entry describes who entered each study, not who recovered without treatment.

lines.q: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?
lines.short: Many do. For alcohol, many people who recovered were never treated. In a US survey, 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer counted as dependent about 3 years later.
lines.but: How many depends on who is counted. Recovery without treatment was measured only for alcohol.
how: Of US soldiers back from Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they'd been dependent on narcotics there, but only about 1 in 100 since coming home. How many got treatment wasn't reported.
In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later. Some still had a few.

Across 21 studies, mostly of people found through treatment, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, depending on how deaths and dropouts are counted. For many, the authors say, the problem is long-lasting.

For alcohol, figures for recovery without treatment run from about 3 to 98 in 100, because studies count different groups. Many who recovered were never treated. Far fewer of everyone with a problem recover untreated in a year.
lines.q_on_site_now: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?

lines.statement: After MDMA, a fall in blood sodium (below 130 mmol/L) with seizures and brain swelling has been reported in mostly young people within hours of taking the drug, in two case series from poison services and in published case reports. These describe a pattern but cannot say how often it happens, because they count only people who became ill and came to a poison service or hospital. In 17 patients aged 15 to 26 (7 men, 10 women) reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (Hartung et al., 2002), sodium on the first day was 107 to 128 mmol/L and all had become ill within 12 hours of taking the drug. A large amount of fluid, alcoholic or not, was known to have been drunk by 10 of the 17 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died; editors' count); for 5 of the 15 who recovered the fluid history was not available. Of those 15, 10 had seizures and 13 were recorded as recovering completely; of the 13 with a stated amount of MDMA, 12 had taken 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to three), and temperature at hospital was recorded as normal in 12 (37.5 degrees Celsius in two, 34.8 in one). Two patients died after brain swelling, a 15-year-old and an 18-year-old, both female, each after one tablet and each having taken MDMA before: one had drunk at least 3 litres of water while dancing, the other water from about two hours after the tablet, with some alcohol; both were given or drank more water after they began to feel ill, arrived at hospital at 32.6 and 33 degrees, and had blood MDMA of 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l. The UK authors note that people had at first been advised to drink plenty of fluids to prevent overheating. In California poison-centre records for 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson et al., 2007), 73 of 188 people with a recorded sodium (about 39 in 100) had a level below 130 mmol/L; 13 of the 545 included cases died, 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing medicines. Hyperthermia was recorded in 40 of the 545 (7.3 in 100) and did not differ clearly between people with and without low sodium (odds ratios 0.58 in women and 0.29 in men, both intervals including 1). In that series MDMA exposure rests on the history given (35 of 103 urine screens were negative for amphetamines but still counted), and the paper gives neither the amount of fluid nor the amount of MDMA. A narrative review of published case reports (Campbell & Rosner, 2008; second-hand, and its table of 32 cases draws 10 rows from the California series) describes more than 25 reports with sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L, most in females aged 15 to 30 after a single dose, including one in which sodium fell from 136 to 130 after 1700 ml of water was drunk following five tablets. A later narrative review (Faria et al., 2020; second-hand, PubMed searched to October 2019 with one author mainly responsible) has 52 table rows about phenethylamine-associated cases, 50 labelled MDMA, and 21 outcomes labelled death. The 36 rows with sodium have lowest values 101–130 mmol/L; one of those rows also reports an earlier value 137, not an extra case. Two pairs of rows appear to repeat cases, although the primary reports were not read; one case cites an unrelated laboratory-methods paper; three fatal rows report neither a numeric sodium result nor hyponatraemia among their effect labels; and one outcome is blank despite a death in the cited title. The authorless 2001 case is traceable, while another row's compound label conflicts with its reference title. Ten fatal rows come from the California series, so the review must not be added to it as an independent 52-person series. Amounts are unknown or blank in 30 rows, including 14 of 21 fatal rows. The review's single-dose statement is restricted to most reported deaths or permanent neurological injuries in women aged 15–30; its table cannot verify that statement. In the 10 fatal rows with sodium, values 109–126 mmol/L lie within the 101–130 range of lowest per-row values in the 24 recovery rows with sodium (editors' counts). The papers explain the fall by MDMA making the body release the water-holding hormone vasopressin, so that water is held back and drinking beyond the body's needs dilutes the sodium; the hormone rise is described from other studies not read here, and the UK authors write that the mechanism remains to be established. Faria also proposes sodium loss in sweat, while describing the drinking reports as anecdotal and the mechanisms as not fully understood. None of the papers read here compared amounts of MDMA or of fluid between people, and the 2020 review bases its drinking discussion on anecdotal reports, so they cannot show whether taking more changes the risk. Blood sodium was not measured in the controlled laboratory sessions of healthy volunteers (Vizeli & Liechti, 2017).
lines.population: Mostly young people who became ill after taking ecstasy (MDMA) and came to a poison service or hospital: 17 patients aged 15 to 26 reported to a UK poisons service over 28 months (1993 to 1996); 545 poison-centre cases in California in 2000 to 2005 (mean age 21), 188 of them with a measured sodium; and published case reports as described in two narrative reviews (more than 25 reports to 2008; 52 tabulated cases to 2018, with errors)
lines.exposure: MDMA sold as ecstasy tablets, content unknown (MDMA confirmed by laboratory tests in 8 of the 15 UK survivors and in both who died; in California by history, with urine screens in 103 of 188 and no specific method), with fluid intake recorded only for some: a large amount in 10 of the 17 UK patients; stated amounts of half a tablet to three tablets in 13 UK survivors; one published case took five tablets (study conditions as reported, not recommendations)
lines.comparator: None for the UK series and the case reports; in California, cases with a sodium of 130 mmol/L or more or reported as normal (115 of 188)
lines.outcome: Serum sodium below 130 mmol/L, seizures, coma, brain swelling, death, and the temperature recorded at hospital
lines.magnitude: UK poisons service, 17 patients over 28 months (Hartung): day 1 sodium 107 to 128 mmol/l; symptoms within 12 hours of the drug in all; large fluid intake known in 10 (8 of the 15 who recovered and both who died), history not available for 5 of the 15; seizures in 10 of the 15 who recovered; 13 of the 15 recorded as recovering completely; temperature at hospital normal in 12 of 15 (37.5 in two, 34.8 in one); 12 of 13 with a stated amount took 2 or fewer tablets (half a tablet to 3); 6 with biochemistry typical of excess antidiuretic hormone; 2 deaths (aged 15 and 18, both female, one tablet each, blood MDMA 0.05 and 0.209 mg/l, temperature 32.6 and 33 degrees Celsius at hospital). California poison control, 545 included cases 2000 to 2005 (Rosenson): sodium recorded in 188 (34.5%); below 130 mmol/L in 73 (about 39 in 100; the text once says 74), median 122 (25th to 75th percentile 119 to 124); 13 deaths in 545 (2.4%), 4 of them in the low-sodium group, all with brain swelling on CT and low blood pressure needing medicines; hyperthermia in 40 of 545 (7.3%), odds ratio for hyperthermia with low sodium against without 0.58 (0.15 to 2.17) in women and 0.29 (0.04 to 2.40) in men; rave party the recorded site for 50 of 545 (9.1%), including 3 of 74 low-sodium cases. Narrative review (Campbell), second-hand: more than 25 case reports, sodium 101 to 130 mEq/L; 32 tabulated cases, 16 deaths. Narrative review (Faria), second-hand: Table 3 has 52 rows (1991–2018), not verified unique cases: 46 female, 21 labelled deaths, 27 recoveries, 3 unknown and 1 blank outcome. Lowest sodium in 36 rows is 101–130 mmol/L, including one with an earlier value 137; 10 fatal rows have 109–126, within the 101–130 range of lowest per-row values in 24 recovery rows. Amount is unknown/blank in 30 rows, including 14/21 fatal rows. Probable duplicates, citation mismatches and unconfirmed fatal low-sodium labels limit interpretation; 10 fatal rows overlap the California series. No rate of low sodium among people who take MDMA can be derived from these counts.
lines.reasoning: Case series start low (observational, no comparison group for the UK series). Risk of bias -1 and imprecision -1 give very low; descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS 6.3). The claim states what was recorded in two poison-service series and, as described in a narrative review, in published case reports, and that none could give a rate. Status replicated: two independent services in two countries show the same pattern; the 2008 review adds nothing independent, because its table draws on the California series and appears to include a UK case that is also in the first series, and the 2020 review (Faria et al.) is not an independent 52-person cohort: its table draws 10 of its 21 labelled deaths from the California series and contains errors (card sc_faria_2020), so it is cited for what it tabulates, with the errors stated. The vasopressin explanation is reported as the papers' explanation and as untested here; it is not part of what the claim asserts. No advice on fluid or on amounts is given.

lines.q: Can drinking lots of water on MDMA lead to low blood salt?
lines.short: Possibly. Low blood salt (sodium) after MDMA has been reported, mostly in young people; of 17 UK cases, at least 10 had drunk a lot of liquid.
lines.but: These only count people who got ill. So they can't show how often it happens, or whether drinking more changes the risk.
how: Over 28 months, 17 people aged 15 to 26 were reported to a UK poisons service. Of the 15 who survived, 10 had seizures, 12 had a normal temperature at hospital, and 13 recovered fully.
The 2 who died, aged 15 and 18, had brain swelling. Both had drunk a lot of water, and drank or were given more after they began to feel ill.
In California poison-centre records, 73 of 188 people who had their blood salt measured had a low level. 4 of those 73 died.
The papers think MDMA makes the body hold on to water, so drinking more than it needs waters down the salt. The UK authors say how it happens is not yet known.
